entries.7159160bb759c86a5938fc401adf37da5f3d3ef3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv118"/><title type="x-ms">Colossians</title> <div sID="gen32027" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Colosse</hi> was a considerable city of Phrygia, and probably not far from Laodicea and Hierapolis; we find these mentioned together, <reference osisRef="Col.4.13">iv. 13</reference>. It is now buried in ruins, and the memory of it chiefly preserved in this epistle. The design of the epistle is to warn them of the danger of the Jewish zealots, who pressed the necessity of observing the ceremonial law; and to fortify them against the mixture of the Gentile philosophy with their Christian principles. He professes a great satisfaction in their stedfastness and constancy, and encourages them to perseverance. It was written about the same time with the epistles to the Ephesians and Philippians, A.D. 62, and in the same place, while he was now a prisoner at Rome. He was not idle in his confinement, and the word of God was not bound. <div eID="gen32028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32029" type="x-p"/> This epistle, like that to the Romans, was written to those he had never seen, nor had any personal acquaintance with. The church planted at Colosse was not by Paul's ministry, but by the ministry of Epaphras or Epaphroditus, an evangelist, one whom he delegated to preach the gospel among the Gentiles; and yet, I. There was a flourishing church at Colosse, and one which was eminent and famous among the churches. One would have thought none would have come to be flourishing churches but those which Paul himself had planted; but here was a flourishing church planted by Epaphras. God is sometimes pleased to make use of the ministry of those who are of less note, and lower gifts, for doing great service to his church. God uses what hands he pleases, and is not tied to those of note, that the <hi type="italic">excellence of the power may appear to be of God and not of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2 Cor. iv. 7</reference>. II. Though Paul had not the planting of this church, yet he did not therefore neglect it; nor, in writing his epistles, does he make any difference between that and other churches. The Colossians, who were converted by the ministry of Epaphras, were as dear to him, and he was as much concerned for their welfare, as the Philippians, or any others who were converted by his ministry. Thus he put an honour upon an inferior minister, and teaches us not to be selfish, nor think all that honour lost which goes beside ourselves. We learn, in his example, not to think it a disparagement to us to water what others have planted, or build upon the foundation which others have laid: as he himself, as a <hi type="italic">wise master-builder, laid the foundation, and another built thereon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">1 Cor. iii. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen32029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32030" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32031" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The inscription, as usual, <reference osisRef="Col.1.1-Col.1.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His thanksgiving to God for what he had heard concerning them—their faith, love, and hope, <reference osisRef="Col.1.3-Col.1.8">ver. 3-8</reference>. III. His prayer for their knowledge, fruitfulness, and strength, <reference osisRef="Col.1.9-Col.1.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. IV. An admirable summary of the Christian doctrine concerning the operation of the Spirit, the person of the Redeemer, the work of redemption, and the preaching of it in the gospel, <reference osisRef="Col.1.12-Col.1.29">ver. 12-29</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv118"/> <div eID="gen32031" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32030" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Inscription and Apostolical Benediction. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timotheus <hi type="italic">our</hi> brother, <hi type="super">2</hi> To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colosse: Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> unto you, and peace, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen32032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32033" type="x-p"/> I. The inscription of this epistle is much the same with the rest; only it is observable that, 1. He calls himself an <hi type="italic">apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God.</hi> An apostle is a prime-minister in the kingdom of Christ, immediately called by Christ, and extraordinarily qualified; his work was peculiarly to plant the Christian church, and confirm the Christian doctrine. He attributes this not to his own merit, strength, or sufficiency; but to the free grace and good-will of God. He thought himself engaged to do his utmost, as an apostle, because he was made so by the will of God. 2. He joins Timothy in commission with himself, which is another instance of his humility; and, though he elsewhere calls him his son (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.1">2 Tim. ii. 1</reference>), yet here he calls him his brother, which is an example to the elder and more eminent ministers to look upon the younger and more obscure as their brethren, and to treat them accordingly with kindness and respect. 3. He calls the Christians at Colosse <hi type="italic">saints, and faithful brethren in Christ.</hi> As all good ministers, so all good Christians, are brethren one to another, who stand in a near relation and owe a mutual love. Towards God they must be saints, consecrated to his honour and sanctified by his grace, bearing his image and aiming at his glory. And in both these, as saints to God and as brethren to one another, they must be faithful. Faithfulness runs through every character and relation of the Christian life, and is the crown and glory of them all. <div eID="gen32033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32034" type="x-p"/> II. The apostolical benediction is the same as usual: <hi type="italic">Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> He wishes them <hi type="italic">grace and peace,</hi> the free favour of God and all the blessed fruits of it; every kind of spiritual blessings, and that <hi type="italic">from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ;</hi> jointly from both, and distinctly from each; as in the former epistle.
entries.48ed226a7dc106e8d1ad4ddeb7037d2c3ca24b1f: <div eID="gen32034" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Thanksgiving for the Colossians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32035" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, <hi type="super">4</hi> Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and of the love <hi type="italic">which ye have</hi> to all the saints, <hi type="super">5</hi> For the hope which is laid up for you in heaven, whereof ye heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel; <hi type="super">6</hi> Which is come unto you, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> in all the world; and bringeth forth fruit, as <hi type="italic">it doth</hi> also in you, since the day ye heard <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> and knew the grace of God in truth: <hi type="super">7</hi> As ye also learned of Epaphras our dear fellowservant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ; <hi type="super">8</hi> Who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit. <div eID="gen32035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32036" type="x-p"/> Here he proceeds to the body of the epistle, and begins with thanksgiving to God for what he had heard concerning them, though he had no personal acquaintance with them, and knew their state and character only by the reports of others. <div eID="gen32036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32037" type="x-p"/> I. He gave thanks to God for them, that they had embraced the gospel of Christ, and given proofs of their fidelity to him. Observe, In his prayers for them he gave thanks for them. Thanksgiving ought to be a part of every prayer; and whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving. Observe, 1. Whom he gives thanks to: <hi type="italic">To God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.</hi> In our thanksgiving we must have an eye to God as God (he is the object of thanksgiving as well as prayer), and is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, in and through whom all good comes to us. He is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ as well as our Father; and it is a matter of encouragement, in all our addresses to God, that we can look to him as Christ's Father and our Father, as his God and our God, <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>. Observe, 2. What he gives thanks to God for—for the graces of God in them, which were evidences of the grace of God towards them: <hi type="italic">Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and of the love you have to all the saints; for the hope which is laid up for you in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.4-Col.1.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Faith, hope, and love, are the three principal graces in the Christian life, and proper matter of our prayer and thanksgiving. (1.) He gives thanks for their faith in Christ Jesus, that they were brought to believe in him, and take upon them the profession of his religion, and venture their souls upon his undertaking. (2.) For their love. Besides the general love which is due to all men, there is a particular love owing to the saints, or those who are of the Christian <hi type="italic">brotherhood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.17">1 Pet. ii. 17</reference>. We must love all the saints, bear an extensive kindness and good-will to good men, notwithstanding smaller points of difference, and many real weaknesses. Some understand it of their charity to the saints in necessity, which is one branch and evidence of Christian love. (3.) For their hope: <hi type="italic">The hope which is laid up for you in heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.5">v. 5</reference>. The happiness of heaven is called their hope, because it is the <hi type="italic">thing hoped for, looking for the blessed hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit. ii. 13</reference>. What is laid out upon believers in this world is much; but what is laid up for them in heaven is much more. And we have reason to give thanks to God for the hope of heaven which good Christians have, or their well-grounded expectation of the future glory. Their faith in Christ, and love to the saints, had an eye to the <hi type="italic">hope laid up for them in heaven.</hi> The more we fix our hopes on the recompence of reward in the other world, the more free and liberal shall we be of our earthly treasure upon all occasions of doing good. <div eID="gen32037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32038" type="x-p"/> II. Having blessed God for these graces, he blesses God for the means of grace which they enjoyed: <hi type="italic">Wherein you heard before in the word of the truth of the gospel.</hi> They had heard in the word of the truth of the gospel concerning this <hi type="italic">hope laid up for them in heaven.</hi> Observe, 1. The gospel is the word of truth, and what we may safely venture our immortal souls upon: it proceeds from the God of truth and the Spirit of truth, and is a faithful saying. He calls it <hi type="italic">the grace of God in truth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">v. 6</reference>. 2. It is a great mercy to hear this word of truth; for the great thing we learn from it is the happiness of heaven. Eternal life is brought to light by the gospel, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.10">2 Tim. i. 10</reference>. They heard of the hope laid up in heaven in the word of the truth of the gospel. "<hi type="italic">Which has come unto you, as it hath to all the world, and bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">v. 6</reference>. This gospel is preached and brings forth fruit in other nations; it has come to you, <hi type="italic">as it hath to all the world,</hi> according to the commission, <hi type="italic">Go preach the gospel in all the nations,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">every creature.</hi>" Observe, (1.) All who hear the word of the gospel ought to bring forth the fruit of the gospel, that is, be obedient to it, and have their principles and lives formed according to it. This was the doctrine first preached: <hi type="italic">Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.3.8">Matt. iii. 8</reference>. And our Lord says, <hi type="italic">If you know these things, happy are you if you do them,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.13.17">John xiii. 17</reference>. Observe, (2.) Wherever the gospel comes, it will bring forth fruit to the honour and glory of God: <hi type="italic">It bringeth forth fruit, as it doth also in you.</hi> We mistake, if we think to monopolize the comforts and benefits of the gospel to ourselves. Does the gospel bring forth fruit in us? So it does in others. <div eID="gen32038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32039" type="x-p"/> III. He takes this occasion to mention the minister by whom they believed (<reference osisRef="Col.1.7-Col.1.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">As you also learned of Epaphras, our dear fellow-servant, who is for you a faithful minister of Christ.</hi> He mentions him with great respect, to engage their love to him. 1. He calls him his fellow-servant, to signify not only that they served the same Master, but that they were engaged in the same work. They were fellow-labourers in the work of the Lord, though one was an apostle and the other an ordinary minister. 2. He calls him his dear fellow-servant: all the servants of Christ ought to love one another, and it is an endearing consideration that they are engaged in the same service. 3. He represents him as one who was a faithful minister of Christ to them, who discharged his trust and fulfilled his ministry among them. Observe, Christ is our proper Master, and we are his ministers. He does not say who is your minister; but <hi type="italic">who is the minister of Christ for you.</hi> It is by his authority and appointment, though for the people's service. 4. He represents him as one who gave them a good word: <hi type="italic">Who also declared unto us your love in the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.8">v. 8</reference>. He recommends him to their affection, from the good report he made of their sincere love to Christ and all his members, which was wrought in them by the Spirit, and is agreeable to the spirit of the gospel. Faithful ministers are glad to be able to speak well of their people.
entries.1def476ef9a6ac0359de5de2c210b789cc62c6ac: <div eID="gen32039" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Prayer for the Colossians. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> For this cause we also, since the day we heard <hi type="italic">it,</hi> do not cease to pray for you, and to desire that ye might be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; <hi type="super">10</hi> That ye might walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God; <hi type="super">11</hi> Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness; <div eID="gen32040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32041" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds in these verses to pray for them. He heard that they were good, and he prayed that they might be better. He was constant in this prayer: <hi type="italic">We do not cease to pray for you.</hi> It may be he could hear of them but seldom, but he constantly prayed for them.—<hi type="italic">And desire that you may be filled with the knowledge,</hi> &c. Observe what it is that he begs of God for them, <div eID="gen32041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32042" type="x-p"/> I. That they might be knowing intelligent Christians: <hi type="italic">filled with the knowledge of his will, in all wisdom and spiritual understanding.</hi> Observe, 1. The knowledge of our duty is the best knowledge. A mere empty notion of the greatest truths is insignificant. Our knowledge of the will of God must be always practical: we must know it, in order to do it. 2. Our knowledge is then a blessing indeed when it is in wisdom, when we know how to apply our general knowledge to our particular occasions, and to suit it to all emergencies. 3. Christians should endeavour to be filled with knowledge; not only to know the will of God, but to know more of it, and to <hi type="italic">increase in the knowledge of God</hi> (as it is <reference osisRef="Col.1.10">v. 10</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.18">2 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen32042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32043" type="x-p"/> II. That their conversation might be good. Good knowledge without a good life will not profit. Our understanding is then a spiritual understanding when we exemplify it in our way of living: <hi type="italic">That you may walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.10">v. 10</reference>), that is, as becomes the relation we stand in to him and the profession we make of him. The agreeableness of our conversation to our religion is pleasing to God as well as to good men. We walk unto all well-pleasing when we walk in all things according to the will of God. <hi type="italic">Being fruitful in every good work.</hi> This is what we should aim at. Good words will not do without good works. We must abound in good works, and in every good work: not in some only, which are more easy, and suitable, and safe, but in all, and every instance of them. There must be a regular uniform regard to all the will of God. And the more fruitful we are in good works the more we shall <hi type="italic">increase in the knowledge of God. He who doeth his will shall know of the doctrine whether it be of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen32043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32044" type="x-p"/> III. That they might be strengthened: <hi type="italic">Strengthened with all might according to his glorious power</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.11">v. 11</reference>), fortified against the temptations of Satan and furnished for all their duty. It is a great comfort to us that he who undertakes to give strength to his people is a God of power and of glorious power. Where there is spiritual life there is still need of spiritual strength, strength for all the actions of the spiritual life. To be strengthened is to be furnished by the grace of God for every good work, and fortified by that grace against every evil one: it is to be enabled to do our duty, and still to hold fast our integrity. The blessed Spirit is the author of this strength; for we are <hi type="italic">strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inward man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Eph. iii. 16</reference>. The word of God is the means of it, by which he conveys it; and it must be fetched in by prayer. It was in answer to earnest prayer that the apostle obtained sufficient grace. In praying for spiritual strength we are not straitened in the promises, and therefore should not be straitened in our own hopes and desires. Observe, 1. He prayed that they might be strengthened with might: this seems a tautology; but he means, that they might be mightily strengthened, or strengthened with might derived from another. 2. It is with all might. It seems unreasonable that a creature should be strengthened with all might, for that is to make him <hi type="italic">almighty;</hi> but he means, with all that might which we have occasion for, to enable us to discharge our duty or preserve our innocence, that grace which is sufficient for us in all the trials of life and able to help us in time of need. 3. It is <hi type="italic">according to his glorious power.</hi> He means, according to the grace of God: but the grace of God in the hearts of believers is the power of God; and there is a glory in this power; it is an excellent and sufficient power. And the communications of strength are not according to our weakness, to whom the strength is communicated, but according to his power, from whom it is received. When God gives he gives like himself, and when he strengthens he strengthens like himself. 4. The special use of this strength was for suffering work: <hi type="italic">That you may be strengthened unto all patience and long-suffering with joyfulness.</hi> He prays not only that they may be <hi type="italic">supported</hi> under their troubles, but <hi type="italic">strengthened</hi> for them: the reason is there is work to be done even when we are suffering. And those who are strengthened <hi type="italic">according to his glorious power</hi> are strengthened, (1.) To all patience. When patience <hi type="italic">hath its perfect work</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.4">Jam. i. 4</reference>) then we are strengthened to all patience—when we not only bear our troubles patiently, but receive them as gifts from God, and are thankful for them. To you <hi type="italic">it is given to suffer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Phil. i. 29</reference>. When we bear our troubles well, though ever so many, and the circumstances of them ever so aggravating, then we bear them with all patience. And the same reason for bearing one trouble will hold for bearing another, if it be a good reason. All patience includes all the kinds of it; not only bearing patience, but waiting patience. (2.) This is even unto long-suffering, that is, drawn out to a great length: not only to bear trouble awhile, but to bear it as long as God pleases to continue it. (3.) It is with joyfulness, to rejoice in tribulation, to take joyfully the spoiling of our goods, and rejoice that we are counted worthy to suffer for his name, to have joy as well as patience in the troubles of life. This we could never do by any strength of our own, but as we are strengthened by the grace of God.
entries.81919f228a63e3d5cbfd15c0d0b386df86dc6e61: <div eID="gen32044" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Redeemer's Dignity; The Work of Redemption; Paul's Preaching. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Giving thanks unto the Father, which hath made us meet to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in light: <hi type="super">13</hi> Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated <hi type="italic">us</hi> into the kingdom of his dear Son: 14 In whom we have redemption through his blood, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the forgiveness of sins: <hi type="super">15</hi> Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: <hi type="super">16</hi> For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether <hi type="italic">they be</hi> thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him: <hi type="super">17</hi> And he is before all things, and by him all things consist. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all <hi type="italic">things</hi> he might have the preeminence. <hi type="super">19</hi> For it pleased <hi type="italic">the Father</hi> that in him should all fulness dwell; 20 And, having made peace through the blood of his cross, by him to reconcile all things unto himself; by him, <hi type="italic">I say,</hi> whether <hi type="italic">they be</hi> things in earth, or things in heaven. <hi type="super">21</hi> And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in <hi type="italic">your</hi> mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled <hi type="super">22</hi> In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight: <hi type="super">23</hi> If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and <hi type="italic">be</hi> not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, <hi type="italic">and</hi> which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister; <hi type="super">24</hi> Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake, which is the church: <hi type="super">25</hi> Whereof I am made a minister, according to the dispensation of God which is given to me for you, to fulfil the word of God; <hi type="super">26</hi> <hi type="italic">Even</hi> the mystery which hath been hid from ages and from generations, but now is made manifest to his saints: <hi type="super">27</hi> To whom God would make known what <hi type="italic">is</hi> the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles; which is Christ in you, the hope of glory: <hi type="super">28</hi> Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus: <hi type="super">29</hi> Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. <div eID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> Here is a summary of the doctrine of the gospel concerning the great work of our redemption by Christ. It comes in here not as the matter of a sermon, but as the matter of a thanksgiving; for our salvation by Christ furnishes us with abundant matter of thanksgiving in every view of it: <hi type="italic">Giving thanks unto the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.12">v. 12</reference>. He does not discourse of the work of redemption in the natural order of it; for then he would speak of the purchase of it first, and afterwards of the application of it. But here he inverts the order, because, in our sense and feeling of it, the application goes before the purchase. We first find the benefits of redemption in our hearts, and then are led by those streams to the original and fountain-head. The order and connection of the apostle's discourse may be considered in the following manner:— <div eID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32047" type="x-p"/> I. He speaks concerning the operations of the Spirit of grace upon us. We must give thanks for them, because by these we are qualified for an interest in the mediation of the Son: <hi type="italic">Giving thanks to the Father,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Col.1.12-Col.1.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. It is spoken of as the work of the Father, because the Spirit of grace is the Spirit of the Father, and the Father works in us by his Spirit. Those in whom the work of grace is wrought must give thanks unto the Father. If we have the comfort of it, he must have the glory of it. Now what is it which is wrought for us in the application of redemption? 1. "He hath <hi type="italic">delivered us from the power of darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.13">v. 13</reference>. He has rescued us from the state of heathenish darkness and wickedness. He hath saved us from the dominion of sin, which is darkness (<reference osisRef="1John.1.6">1 John i. 6</reference>), from the dominion of Satan, who is the <hi type="italic">prince of darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>), and from the damnation of hell, which is <hi type="italic">utter darkness,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">Matt. xxv. 30</reference>. They are <hi type="italic">called out of darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. ii. 9</reference>. 2. "He hath <hi type="italic">translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son,</hi> brought us into the gospel-state, and made us members of the church of Christ, which is a state of light and purity." <hi type="italic">You were once darkness, but now are you light in the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. ii. 9</reference>. Those were made willing subjects of Christ who were the slaves of Satan. The conversion of a sinner is the translation of a soul into the kingdom of Christ out of the kingdom of the devil. The power of sin is shaken off, and the power of Christ submitted to. The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus makes them free from the law of sin and death; and it is the kingdom of his dear Son, or the Son of his peculiar love, his beloved Son (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>), and eminently the beloved, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Eph. i. 6</reference>. 3. "He hath not only done this, but hath <hi type="italic">made us meet to partake of the inheritance of the saints in light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.12">v. 12</reference>. He hath prepared us for the eternal happiness of heaven, as the Israelites divided the promised land by lot; and has given us the earnest and assurance of it." This he mentions first because it is the first indication of the future blessedness, that by the grace of God we find ourselves in some measure prepared for it. God gives <hi type="italic">grace and glory,</hi> and we are here told what they both are. (1.) What that glory is. It is the <hi type="italic">inheritance of the saints in light.</hi> It is an inheritance, and belongs to them as children, which is the best security and the sweetest tenure: <hi type="italic">If children, then heirs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Rom. viii. 17</reference>. And it is an inheritance of the saints-proper to sanctified souls. Those who are not saints on earth will never be saints in heaven. And it is an inheritance in light; the perfection of knowledge, holiness, and joy, by communion with God, who is light, and the Father of lights, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jam. i. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.5">John i. 5</reference>. (2.) What this grace is. It is a meetness for the inheritance: "<hi type="italic">He hath made us meet to be partakers,</hi> that is, suited and fitted us for the heavenly state by a proper temper and habit of soul; and he makes us meet by the powerful influence of his Spirit." It is the effect of the divine power to change the heart, and make it heavenly. Observe, All who are designed for heaven hereafter are prepared for heaven now. As those who live and die unsanctified go out of the world with their hell about them, so those who are sanctified and renewed go out of the world with their heaven about them. Those who have the inheritance of sons have the education of sons and the disposition of sons: they <hi type="italic">have the Spirit of adoption, whereby they cry, Abba, Father.</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Rom. viii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">And, because you are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Gal. iv. 6</reference>. This meetness for heaven is the earnest of the Spirit in our heart, which is part of payment, and assures the full payment. Those who are sanctified shall be glorified (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Rom. viii. 30</reference>), and will be for ever indebted to the grace of God, which hath sanctified them. <div eID="gen32047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32048" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning the person of the Redeemer. Glorious things are here said of him; for blessed Paul was full of Christ, and took all occasions to speak honourably of him. He speaks of him distinctly as God, and as Mediator. 1. As God he speaks of him, <reference osisRef="Col.1.15-Col.1.17">v. 15-17</reference>. (1.) He is the <hi type="italic">image of the invisible God.</hi> Not as man was made <hi type="italic">in the image of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Gen. i. 27</reference>), in his natural faculties and dominion over the creatures: no, he is the <hi type="italic">express image of his person,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. He is so the image of God as the son is the image of his father, who has a natural likeness to him; so that he who has seen him has <hi type="italic">seen the Father,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">glory was the glory of the only-begotten of the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.14">John i. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.9">xiv. 9</reference>. (2.) He is the <hi type="italic">first-born of every creature.</hi> Not that he is himself a creature; for it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prototokos pases ktiseos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">born</hi> or <hi type="italic">begotten before all the creation,</hi> or before any creature was made, which is the scripture-way of representing eternity, and by which the eternity of God is represented to us: <hi type="italic">I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, or ever the earth was; when there was no depth, before the mountains were settled, while as yet he had not made the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.23-Prov.8.26">Prov. viii. 23-26</reference>. It signifies his dominion over all things, as the first-born in a family is heir and lord of all, so he is the <hi type="italic">heir of all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">Heb. i. 2</reference>. The word, with only the change of the accent, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">prototokos,</hi></hi> signifies actively the first begetter or producer of all things, and so it well agrees with the following clause. <hi type="italic">Vid. Isidor. Peleus. epist.</hi> 30 <hi type="italic">lib.</hi> 3. (3.) He is so far from beginning himself a creature that he is the Creator: <hi type="italic">For by him were all things created, which are in heaven and earth, visible and invisible,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">v. 16</reference>. He made all things out of nothing, the highest angel in heaven, as well as men upon earth. He made the world, the upper and lower world, with all the inhabitants of both. <hi type="italic">All things were made by him, and without him was not any thing made which was made,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.3">John i. 3</reference>. He speaks here as if there were several orders of angels: <hi type="italic">Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers,</hi> which must signify either different degrees of excellence or different offices and employments. <hi type="italic">Angels, authorities, and powers,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1 Pet. iii. 22</reference>. Christ is the eternal wisdom of the Father, and the world was made in wisdom. He is the eternal Word, and the world was made by the word of God. He is the <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord,</hi> and the world was made by that arm. <hi type="italic">All things are created by him and for him;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">di autou kai eis auton.</hi></hi> Being created by him, they were created for him; being made by his power, they were made according to his pleasure and for his praise. He is the end, as well as the cause of all things. <hi type="italic">To him are all things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.36">Rom. xi. 36</reference>; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eis auton ta panta.</hi></hi> (4.) He <hi type="italic">was before all things.</hi> He had a being before the world was made, before the beginning of time, and therefore from all eternity. Wisdom was with the Father, and possessed by him in the beginning of his ways, before his works of old, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Prov. viii. 22</reference>. And in the beginning the Word was with God and was God, <reference osisRef="John.1.1">John i. 1</reference>. He not only had a being before he was born of the virgin, but he had a being before all time. (5.) <hi type="italic">By him all things consist.</hi> They not only subsist in their beings, but consist in their order and dependences. He not only created them all at first, but it is by the word of his power that they are still upheld, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. The whole creation is kept together by the power of the Son of God, and made to consist in its proper frame. It is preserved from disbanding and running into confusion. <div eID="gen32048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32049" type="x-p"/> 2. The apostle next shows what he is as Mediator, <reference osisRef="Col.1.18-Col.1.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. (1.) He is the <hi type="italic">head of the body the church:</hi> not only a head of government and direction, as the king is the head of the state and has right to prescribe laws, but a head of vital influence, as the head in the natural body: for all grace and strength are derived from him: and the church is his body, <hi type="italic">the fulness of him who filleth all in all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22-Eph.1.23">Eph. i. 22, 23</reference>. (2.) He is the <hi type="italic">beginning, the first-born from the dead,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">arche, prototokos</hi></hi>—the principle, the first-born from the dead; the principle of our resurrection, as well as the first-born himself. All our hopes and joys take their rise from him who is the author of our salvation. Not that he was the first who ever rose from the dead, but the first and only one who rose by his own power, and was <hi type="italic">declared to be the Son of God, and Lord of all things.</hi> And he is the head of the resurrection, and has given us an example and evidence of our resurrection from the dead. He rose as the first-fruits, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1 Cor. xv. 20</reference>. (3.) He hath in <hi type="italic">all things the pre-eminence.</hi> It was the will of the Father that he should have <hi type="italic">all power in heaven and earth,</hi> that he might be preferred above angels and all the powers in heaven (he has <hi type="italic">obtained a more excellent name than they,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">Heb. i. 4</reference>), and that in all the affairs of the kingdom of God among men he should have the pre-eminence. He has the pre-eminence in the hearts of his people above the world and the flesh; and by giving him the pre-eminence we comply with the Father's will, That <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.23">John v. 23</reference>. (4.) All fulness dwells in him, and it pleased the Father it should do so (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">v. 19</reference>), not only a fulness of abundance for himself, but redundance for us, a fulness of merit and righteousness, of strength and grace. As the head is the seat and source of the animal spirits, so is Christ of all graces to his people. <hi type="italic">It pleased the Father</hi> that all fulness should dwell in him; and we may have free resort to him for all that grace for which we have occasion. He not only intercedes for it, but is the trustee in whose hands it is lodged to dispense to us: <hi type="italic">Of his fulness we receive, and grace for grace,</hi> grace in us answering to that grace which is in him (<reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>), and <hi type="italic">he fills all in all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.1.23">Eph. i. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen32049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32050" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning the work of redemption. He speaks of the nature of it, or wherein it consists; and of the means of it, by which it was procured. <div eID="gen32050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32051" type="x-p"/> 1. Wherein it consists. It is made to lie in two things:—(1.) In the remission of sin: <hi type="italic">In whom we have redemption, even the forgiveness of sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.14">v. 14</reference>. It was sin which sold us, sin which enslaved us: if we are redeemed, we must be redeemed from sin; and this is by forgiveness, or remitting the obligation to punishment. So <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Eph. i. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">In whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.</hi> (2.) In reconciliation to God. God by him <hi type="italic">reconciled all things to himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">v. 20</reference>. He is the Mediator of reconciliation, who procures peace as well as pardon for sinners, who brings them into a state of friendship and favour at present, and will bring all holy creatures, angels as well as men, into one glorious and blessed society at last: <hi type="italic">things in earth, or things in heaven.</hi> So <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">He will gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven and which are on earth.</hi> The word is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">anakephalaiosasthai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he will bring them all under one head.</hi> The Gentiles, who were alienated, and <hi type="italic">enemies in their minds by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.21">v. 21</reference>. Here see what was their condition by nature, and in their Gentile state—estranged from God, and at enmity with God: and yet this <hi type="italic">enmity is slain,</hi> and, notwithstanding this distance, we are now reconciled. Christ has laid the foundation for our reconciliation; for he has paid the price of it, has purchased the proffer and promise of it, proclaims it as a prophet, applies it as a king. Observe, The greatest enemies to God, who have stood at the greatest distance and bidden him defiance, may be reconciled, if it by not their own fault. <div eID="gen32051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32052" type="x-p"/> 2. How the redemption is procured: <hi type="italic">it is through his blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.14">v. 14</reference>); he has <hi type="italic">made peace through the blood of his cross</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">v. 20</reference>), and it is <hi type="italic">in the body of his flesh through death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.22">v. 22</reference>. It was the <hi type="italic">blood which made an atonement, for the blood is the life; and without the shedding of blood there is no remission,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.22">Heb. ix. 22</reference>. There was such a value in the blood of Christ that, on account of Christ's shedding it, God was willing to deal with men upon new terms to bring them under a covenant of grace, and <hi type="italic">for his sake,</hi> and in consideration of his death upon the cross, to pardon and accept to favour all who comply with them. <div eID="gen32052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32053" type="x-p"/> IV. Concerning the preaching of this redemption. Here observe, <div eID="gen32053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32054" type="x-p"/> 1. To whom it was preached: <hi type="italic">To every creature under heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.23">v. 23</reference>), that is, it was ordered to be preached to every creature, <reference osisRef="Mark.16.15">Mark xvi. 15</reference>. It may be preached to every creature; for the gospel excludes none who do not exclude themselves. More or less it has been or will be preached to every nation, though many have sinned away the light of it and perhaps some have never yet enjoyed it. <div eID="gen32054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32055" type="x-p"/> 2. By whom it was preached: <hi type="italic">Whereof I Paul am made a minister.</hi> Paul was a great apostle; but he looks upon it as the highest of his titles of honour to be a minister of the gospel of Jesus Christ. Paul takes all occasions to speak of his office; for he <hi type="italic">magnified his office,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.13">Rom. xi. 13</reference>. And again in <reference osisRef="Col.1.25">v. 25</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whereof I am made a minister.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen32055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32056" type="x-p"/> (1.) Whence Paul had his ministry: it was <hi type="italic">according to the dispensation of God which was given to him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.25">v. 25</reference>), the economy or wise disposition of things in the house of God. He was steward and master-builder, and this was given to him: he did not usurp it, nor take it to himself; and he could not challenge it as a debt. He received it from God as a gift, and took it as a favour. <div eID="gen32056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32057" type="x-p"/> (2.) For whose sake he had his ministry: "<hi type="italic">It is for you,</hi> for your benefit: <hi type="italic">ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">2 Cor. iv. 5</reference>. We are Christ's ministers for the good of his people, to <hi type="italic">fulfil the word of God</hi> (that is, fully to preach it), of which you will have the greater advantage. The more we fulfil our ministry, or fill up all the parts of it, the greater will be the benefit of the people; they will be the more filled with knowledge, and furnished for service." <div eID="gen32057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32058" type="x-p"/> (3.) What kind of preacher Paul was. This is particularly represented. <div eID="gen32058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32059" type="x-p"/> [1.] He was a suffering preacher: <hi type="italic">Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">v. 24</reference>. He suffered in the cause of Christ, and for the good of the church. He suffered for preaching the gospel to them. And, while he suffered in so good a cause, he could rejoice in his sufferings, <hi type="italic">rejoice that he was counted worthy to suffer,</hi> and esteem it an honour to him. <hi type="italic">And fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh.</hi> Not that the afflictions of Paul, or any other, were expiations for sin, as the sufferings of Christ were. There was nothing wanting in them, nothing which needed to <hi type="italic">be filled up.</hi> They were perfectly sufficient to answer the intention of them, the satisfaction of God's justice, in order to the salvation of his people. But the sufferings of Paul and other good ministers made them conformable to Christ; and they followed him in his suffering state: so they are said to fill up what was behind of the sufferings of Christ, as the wax fills up the vacuities of the seal, when it receives the impression of it. Or it may be meant not of Christ's sufferings, but of his suffering for Christ. He <hi type="italic">filled that which was behind.</hi> He had a certain rate and measure of suffering for Christ assigned him; and, as his sufferings were agreeable to that appointment, so he was still filling up more and more what was behind, or remained of them to his share. <div eID="gen32059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32060" type="x-p"/> [2.] He was a close preacher: he preached not only in public, but <hi type="italic">from house to house,</hi> from person to person. <hi type="italic">Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">v. 28</reference>. Every man has need to be warned and taught, and therefore let every man have his share. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> When we warn people of what they do amiss, we must teach them to do better: warning and teaching must go together. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Men must be warned and taught in all wisdom. We must choose the fittest seasons, and use the likeliest means, and accommodate ourselves to the different circumstances and capacities of those we have to do with, and teach them as they are able to bear. That which he aimed at was to <hi type="italic">present every man perfect in Christ Jesus,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">teleios,</hi></hi> either perfect in the knowledge of the Christian doctrine (<hi type="italic">Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, be thus minded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">Phil. iii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2 Tim. iii. 17</reference>), or else crowned with a glorious reward hereafter, when he will <hi type="italic">present to himself a glorious church</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Eph. v. 27</reference>), and bring them to the <hi type="italic">spirits of just men made perfect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">Heb. xii. 23</reference>. Observe, Ministers ought to aim at the improvement and salvation of every particular person who hears them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He was a laborious preacher, and one who took pains: he was no loiter, and did not do his work negligently (<reference osisRef="Col.1.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.</hi> He laboured and strove, used great diligence and contended with many difficulties, according to the measure of grace afforded to him and the extraordinary presence of Christ which was with him. Observe, As Paul laid out himself to do much good, so he had this favour, that the power of God wrought in him the more effectually. The more we labour in the work of the Lord the greater measures of help we may expect from him in it (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.7">Eph. iii. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">According to the gift of the grace of God given unto me, by the effectual working of his power.</hi> <div eID="gen32060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32061" type="x-p"/> 3. The gospel which was preached. We have an account of this: <hi type="italic">Even the mystery which hath been hid from ages, and from generations, but is now made manifest to his saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.26-Col.1.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Observe, (1.) The mystery of the gospel was long hidden: it was concealed from ages and generations, the several ages of the church under the Old-Testament dispensation. They were in a state of minority, and training up for a more perfect state of things, and could not look to the end of those things which were ordained, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>. (2.) This mystery now, in the fulness of time, is made manifest to the saints, or clearly revealed and made apparent. The veil which was over Moses's face is done away in Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2 Cor. iii. 14</reference>. The meanest saint under the gospel understands more than the greatest prophets under the law. He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than they. The <hi type="italic">mystery of Christ, which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.4-Eph.3.5">Eph. iii. 4, 5</reference>. And what is this mystery? It is the riches of God's glory among the Gentiles. The peculiar doctrine of the gospel was a mystery which was before hidden, and is now made manifest and made known. But the great mystery here referred to is the breaking down of the partition-wall between the Jew and Gentile, and preaching the gospel to the Gentile world, and making those partakers of the privileges of the gospel state who before lay in ignorance and idolatry: <hi type="italic">That the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs, and of the same body, and partakers together of his promise in Christ by the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Eph. iii. 6</reference>. This mystery, thus made known, <hi type="italic">is Christ in you</hi> (or among you) <hi type="italic">the hope of glory.</hi> Observe, Christ is the hope of glory. The ground of our hope is Christ in the word, or the gospel revelation, declaring the nature and methods of obtaining it. The evidence of our hope is Christ in the heart, or the sanctification of the soul, and its preparation for the heavenly glory. <div eID="gen32061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32062" type="x-p"/> 4. The duty of those who are interested in this redemption: <hi type="italic">If you continue in the faith, grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel which you have heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">v. 23</reference>. We must continue in the faith grounded and settled, and not be moved away from the hope of the gospel; that is, we must be so well fixed in our minds as not to be moved from it by any temptations. We must be stedfast and immovable (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.58">1 Cor. xv. 58</reference>) and <hi type="italic">hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">Heb. x. 23</reference>. Observe, We can expect the happy end of our faith only when we continue in the faith, and are so far grounded and settled in it as not to be moved from it. We must not <hi type="italic">draw back unto perdition,</hi> but <hi type="italic">believe unto the saving of the soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">Heb. x. 39</reference>. We must be faithful to death, through all trials, that we may receive the <hi type="italic">crown of life, and receive the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.9">1 Pet. i. 9</reference>.  <chapter eID="Col.1"/> <div eID="gen32062" type="x-p"/>

entries.92f143ecb36c8f54d242e351232657c33fc2aa85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17825"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen36201" type="x-p"/> The GENUINENESS of this Epistle is attested by Justin Martyr [Dialogue with Trypho, p. 311, B.], who quotes "the first-born of every creature," in reference to Christ, from <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>. Theophilus of Antioch [To Autolychus, 2, p. 100]. Irenæus [Against Heresies, 3.14.1], quotes expressly from this "Epistle to the Colossians" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>). Clement of Alexandria [Miscellanies, 1. p. 325], quotes <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>; also elsewhere he quotes Col 1:9-11, 28; 2:2, &c.; <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">3</reference>, &c. Tertullian [The Prescription against Heretics, 7], quotes <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>; [On the Resurrection of the Flesh, 23], and quotes <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>, 20; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>. Origen [Against Celsus, 5.8], quotes <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, 19.<div eID="gen36201" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen36200" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen36202" type="x-p"/> Colosse (or, as it is spelt in the best manuscripts, "Colassæ") was a city of Phrygia, on the river Lycus, a branch of the Meander. The Church there was mainly composed of Gentiles (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.13">Col 2:13</reference>). Alford infers from <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>), that Paul had not seen its members, and therefore could not have been its founder, as Theodoret thought. <reference osisRef="Col.1.7">Col 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference> suggests the probability that Epaphras was the first founder of the Church there. The date of its foundation must have been subsequent to Paul's visitation, "strengthening in order" all the churches of Galatia and Phrygia (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.24">Ac 18:24</reference>); for otherwise we must have visited the Colossians, which <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference> implies he had not. Had Paul been their father in the faith, he would doubtless have alluded to the fact, as in <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.6">1Co 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.5">1Th 1:5</reference>; 2:1. It is only in the Epistles, Romans and Ephesians, and this Epistle, such allusions are wanting; in that to the Romans, because, as in this Church of Colosse, he had not been the instrument of their conversion; in that to the Ephesians, owing to the general nature of the Epistle. Probably during the "two years" of Paul's stay at Ephesus, when "all which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.10">Ac 19:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.26">26</reference>), Epaphras, Philemon, Archippus, Apphia and the other natives of Colosse, becoming converted at Ephesus, were subsequently the first sowers of the Gospel seed in their own city. This will account for their personal acquaintance with, and attachment to, Paul and his fellow ministers, and for his loving language as to them, and their counter salutations to him. So also with respect to "them at Laodicea," (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36203" type="x-p"/> The OBJECT of the Epistle is to counteract Jewish false teaching, by setting before the Colossians their true standing in Christ alone (exclusive of all other heavenly beings), the majesty of His person, and the completeness of the redemption wrought by Him; hence they ought to be conformed to their risen Lord, and to exhibit that conformity in all the relations of ordinary life <reference osisRef="Col.2.16">Col 2:16</reference>, "new moon, sabbath days," shows that the false teaching opposed in this Epistle is that of Judaizing Christians. These mixed up with pure Christianity Oriental theosophy and angel-worship, and the asceticism of certain sections of the Jews, especially the Essenes. Compare Josephus [Wars of the Jews, 2.8,13]. These theosophists promised to their followers a deeper insight into the world of spirits, and a nearer approach to heavenly purity and intelligence, than the simple Gospel affords. Conybeare and Howson think that some Alexandrian Jew had appeared at Colosse, imbued with the Greek philosophy of Philo's school, combining with it the Rabbinical theosophy and angelology which afterwards was embodied in the Cabbala. Compare Josephus [Antiquities, 12.3,4], from which we know that Alexander the Great had garrisoned the towns of Lydia and Phrygia with two thousand Mesopotamian and Babylonian Jews in the time of a threatened revolt. The Phrygians themselves had a mystic tendency in their worship of Cybele, which inclined them to receive the more readily the incipient Gnosticism of Judaizers, which afterward developed itself into the strangest heresies. In the Pastoral Epistles, the evil is spoken of as having reached a more deadly phase (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.3.6">1Ti 4:1-3; 6</reference>:5), whereas he brings no charge of immorality in this Epistle: a proof of its being much earlier in date.<div eID="gen36203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36204" type="x-p"/> The PLACE from which it was written seems to have been Rome, during his first imprisonment there (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.17-Acts.28.31">Ac 28:17-31</reference>). In my Introduction to the Epistle to the Ephesians, it was shown that the three Epistles, Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon, were sent at the same time, namely, during the freer portion of his imprisonment, before the death of Burrus. <reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">20</reference>, imply greater freedom than he had while writing to the Philippians, after the promotion of Tigellinus to be Prætorian Prefect. See Introduction to Philippians.<div eID="gen36204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36205" type="x-p"/> This Epistle, though carried by the same bearer, Tychicus, who bore that to the Ephesians, was written previously to that Epistle; for many phrases similar in both appear in the more expanded form in the Epistle to the Ephesians (compare also Note, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Ep 6:21</reference>). The Epistle to the Laodiceans (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>) was written before that to the Colossians, but probably was sent by him to Laodicea at the same time with that to the Church at Colosse.<div eID="gen36205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36206" type="x-p"/> The STYLE is peculiar: many Greek phrases occur here, found nowhere else. Compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>, "spoil you"; "making a show of them openly" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>); "beguile of your reward," and "intruding" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>); "will-worship"; "satisfying" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>); "filthy communication" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.8">Col 3:8</reference>); "rule" (<reference osisRef="Col.3.15">Col 3:15</reference>); "comfort" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.11">Col 4:11</reference>). The loftiness and artificial elaboration of style correspond to the majestic nature of his theme, the majesty of Christ's person and office, in contrast to the beggarly system of the Judaizers, the discussion of which was forced on him by the controversy. Hence arises his use of unusual phraseology. On the other hand, in the Epistle of the Ephesians, subsequently written, in which he was not so hampered by the exigencies of controversy, he dilates on the same glorious truths, so congenial to him, more at large, freely and uncontroversially, in the fuller outpouring of his spirit, with less of the elaborate and antithetical language of system, such as was needed in cautioning the Colossians against the particular errors threatening them. Hence arises the striking similarity of many of the phrases in the two Epistles written about the same time, and generally in the same vein of spiritual thought; while the peculiar phrases of the Epistle to the Colossians are such as are natural, considering the controversial purpose of that Epistle.<div eID="gen36206" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Col.1.1-Col.1.29">Col 1:1-29</reference>. Address: Introduction: Confirming Epaphras' Teaching: The Glories of Christ: Thanksgiving and Prayer for the Colossians: His Own Ministry of the Mystery.</title> <div sID="gen36207" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17825"/><hi type="bold">1. by the will of God--</hi>Greek, "through," &c. (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.1">1Co 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Timothy--</hi>(Compare Notes, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Phil.1.1">Php 1:1</reference>). He was with Paul at the time of writing in Rome. He had been companion of Paul in his first tour through Phrygia, in which Colosse was. Hence the Colossians seem to have associated him with Paul in their affections, and the apostle joins him with himself in the address. Neither, probably, had seen the Colossian Church (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>); but had seen, during their tour through Phrygia, individual Colossians, as Epaphras, Philemon, Archippus, and Apphia (Phm 2), who when converted brought the Gospel to their native city. <div eID="gen36208" type="x-p"/>
entries.67a8466ed81578645856f90d4942541131cf6de5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17826"/><div sID="gen36209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17826"/><hi type="bold">2. Colosse--</hi>written in the oldest manuscripts, "Colasse." As "saints" implies union with God, so "the faithful brethren" union with Christian men [Bengel].<div eID="gen36209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Lord Jesus Christ--</hi>supported by some oldest manuscripts omitted by others of equal antiquity. <div eID="gen36210" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f5fb2d77456b818ec3dff7cb6b75942ff253a4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17827"/><div sID="gen36211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17827"/>3. Thanksgiving for the "faith, hope, and love" of the Colossians. So in the twin Epistle sent at the same time and by the same bearer, Tychicus (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.15">Ep 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen36211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We--</hi>I and Timothy.<div eID="gen36212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the Father--</hi>So some of the oldest manuscripts read. But others better omit the "and," which probably crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Ep 1:3</reference>.<div eID="gen36213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">praying always for you--</hi>with thanksgiving (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>). See <reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference>. <div eID="gen36214" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c5e84db3d41736db3ea404d121214f9d2736a58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17828"/><div sID="gen36215" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17828"/><hi type="bold">4. Since we heard--</hi>literally, "Having heard." The language implies that he had only heard of, and not seen, them (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.8">Ro 1:8</reference>, where like language is used of a Church which he had not at the time visited.<div eID="gen36215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love ... to all--</hi>the absent, as well as those present [Bengel]. <div eID="gen36216" type="x-p"/>
entries.517c8ad77327878b47fab17a1c95bdc4d38452bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17829"/><div sID="gen36217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17829"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>to be joined with the words immediately preceding: "The love which ye have to all the saints because of (literally, 'on account of') the hope," &c. The hope of eternal life will never be in us an inactive principle but will always produce "love." This passage is abused by Romanists, as if the hope of salvation depended upon works. A false argument. It does not follow that our hope is founded on our works because we are strongly stimulated to live well; since nothing is more effectual for this purpose than the sense of God's free grace [Calvin].<div eID="gen36217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid up--</hi>a treasure laid up so as to be out of danger of being lost (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). Faith, love, and hope (<reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>), comprise the sum of Christianity. Compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>, "the hope of the Gospel."<div eID="gen36218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in heaven--</hi>Greek, "in the heavens."<div eID="gen36219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereof ye heard before--</hi>namely, at the time when it was preached to you.<div eID="gen36220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the word, &c.--</hi>That "hope" formed part of "the word of the truth of the Gospel" (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.13">Ep 1:13</reference>), that is, part of the Gospel truth preached unto you. <div eID="gen36221" type="x-p"/>
entries.64a7fbef09258871d7ee1337e41674b0dfabdc5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17830"/><div sID="gen36222" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17830"/><hi type="bold">6. Which is come unto you--</hi>Greek, "Which is present among you," that is, which has come to, and remains with, you. He speaks of the word as a living person present among them.<div eID="gen36222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as it is in all the world--</hi>virtually, as it was by this time preached in the leading parts of the then known world; potentially, as Christ's command was that the Gospel should be preached to all nations, and not be limited, as the law was, to the Jews (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.38">Mt 13:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">24:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19">28:19</reference>). However, the true reading, and that of the oldest manuscripts, is that which omits the following "and," thus (the "it is" of English Version is not in the original Greek): "As in all the world it is bringing forth fruit and growing (so the oldest manuscripts read; English Version omits 'and growing,' without good authority), even as it doth in you also." Then what is asserted is not that the Gospel has been preached in all the world, but that it is bearing fruits of righteousness, and (like a tree growing at the same time that it is bearing fruit) growing in numbers of its converts in, or throughout, all the world.<div eID="gen36223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard of it--</hi>rather, "heard it."<div eID="gen36224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and knew--</hi>rather, "came to know"; became fully experimentally acquainted with.<div eID="gen36225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the grace of God in truth--</hi>that is, in its truth, and with true knowledge [Alford]. <div eID="gen36226" type="x-p"/>
entries.339e250716d84fbececb1ec7ac60a2506142168d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17831"/><div sID="gen36227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17831"/><hi type="bold">7. As ye also learned--</hi>"Also" is omitted in the oldest manuscripts. The insertion implied that those inserting it thought that Paul had preached the Gospel to the Colossians as well as Epaphras, Whereas the omission in the oldest manuscripts implies that Epaphras alone was the founder of the Church at Colosse.<div eID="gen36227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>"from Epaphras."<div eID="gen36228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dear--</hi>Greek, "beloved."<div eID="gen36229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fellow servant--</hi>namely, of Christ. In Phm 23 he calls him "my fellow prisoner." It is possible that Epaphras may have been apprehended for his zealous labors in Asia Minor; but more probable that Paul gave him the title; as his faithful companion in his imprisonment (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, as to Meyer's conjecture).<div eID="gen36230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who is for you, &c.--</hi>Translate, "who is faithful in your behalf as a minister of Christ"; hinting that he is one not to be set aside for the new and erroneous teachers (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1-Col.2.23">Col 2:1-23</reference>). Most of the oldest manuscripts read, "for (or 'in behalf of') US." Vulgate, however, with one of the oldest manuscripts, supports English Version. <div eID="gen36231" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb8ec27916d79cee79055424400f0a1d8626eb51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17832"/><div sID="gen36232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17832"/><hi type="bold">8. your love--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference>); "to all the saints."<div eID="gen36232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Spirit--</hi>the sphere or element IN which alone true love is found; as distinguished from the state of those "in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.9">Ro 8:9</reference>). Yet even they needed to be stirred up to greater love (<reference osisRef="Col.3.12-Col.3.14">Col 3:12-14</reference>). Love is the first and chief fruit of the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>). <div eID="gen36233" type="x-p"/>
entries.86aaf9e08750e97f42645dbfe2c8385274280261: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17833"/><div sID="gen36234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17833"/><hi type="bold">9. we also--</hi>on our part.<div eID="gen36234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pray--</hi>Here he states what in particular he prays for; as in <reference osisRef="Col.1.3">Col 1:3</reference> he stated generally the fact of his praying for them.<div eID="gen36236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to desire--</hi>"to make request."<div eID="gen36237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">might be filled--</hi>rather, "may be filled"; a verb, often found in this Epistle (<reference osisRef="Col.4.12">Col 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen36238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowledge--</hi>Greek, "full and accurate knowledge." Akin to the Greek for "knew" (see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of his will--</hi>as to how ye ought to walk (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.17">Ep 5:17</reference>); as well as chiefly that "mystery of His will, according to His good pleasure which He purposed in Himself; that in the fulness of times He might gather together in one all things in Christ" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>); God's "will," whereby He eternally purposed to reconcile to Himself, and save men by Christ, not by angels, as the false teachers in some degree taught (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>) [Estius]. There seems to have been a want of knowledge among the Colossians; notwithstanding their general excellencies; hence he so often dwells on this subject (<reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.2">Col 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.10">3:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">6</reference>). On the contrary he less extols wisdom to the Corinthians, who were puffed up with the conceit of knowledge.<div eID="gen36240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wisdom--</hi>often mentioned in this Epistle, as opposed to the (false) "philosophy" and "show of wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>, 23; compare <reference osisRef="Eph.1.8">Ep 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>sagacity to discern what on each occasion is suited to the place and the time; its seat is "the understanding" or intellect; wisdom is more general and has its seat in the whole compass of the faculties of the soul [Bengel]. "Wouldst thou know that the matters in the word of Christ are real things? Then never read them for mere knowledge sake" [Quoted by Gaussen.] Knowledge is desirable only when seasoned by "spiritual understanding." <div eID="gen36242" type="x-p"/>
entries.5781e5bd72fdc82b84fe228d780e10b374bfaba0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17834"/><div sID="gen36243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17834"/>10. Greek, "So as to walk"; so that ye may walk. True knowledge of God's will is inseparable from walking conformably to it.<div eID="gen36243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worthy of the Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Ep 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>so as in every way to be well-pleasing to God.<div eID="gen36245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasing--</hi>literally, "desire of pleasing."<div eID="gen36246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being fruitful--</hi>Greek, "bearing fruit." This is the first manifestation of their "walking worthy of the Lord." The second is, "increasing (growing) in the knowledge of God (or as the oldest manuscripts read, 'growing BY the full knowledge of God')"; thus, as the Gospel word (<reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference>) was said to "bring forth fruit," and to "grow" in all the world, even as it did in the Colossians, ever since the day they knew the grace of God, so here it is Paul's prayer that they might continue to "bring forth fruit," and "grow" more and more by the full knowledge of God, the more that "knowledge" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>) was imparted to them. The full knowledge of God is the real instrument of enlargement in soul and life of the believer [Alford]. The third manifestation of their walk is (<reference osisRef="Col.1.11">Col 1:11</reference>), "Being strengthened with all might," &c. The fourth is (<reference osisRef="Col.1.12">Col 1:12</reference>), "Giving thanks unto the Father," &c. <div eID="gen36247" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9ed9bd42ea09855428a2d24eee1b05ea0a369fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17835"/><div sID="gen36248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17835"/>11. Greek, "Being made mighty with (literally, 'in') all might."<div eID="gen36248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his glorious power--</hi>rather, "according to the power (the characteristic of 'His glory,' here appropriate to Paul's argument, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.19">Ep 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.10">6:10</reference>; as its exuberant 'riches,' in <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16">Ep 3:16</reference>) of His glory." His power is inseparable from His glory (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.4">Ro 6:4</reference>).<div eID="gen36249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto all patience--</hi>so as to attain to all patient endurance; persevering, enduring continuance in the faith, in spite of trials of persecutors, and seductions of false teachers.<div eID="gen36250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long-suffering--</hi>towards those whom one could repel. "Patience," or "endurance," is exercised in respect to those whom one cannot repel [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen36251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36252" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with joyfulness--</hi>joyful endurance (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen36252" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bc26a3ea1bf6ed1837c1135d427f71980d300e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17836"/><div sID="gen36253" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17836"/>12. You "giving thanks unto the Father." See on <reference osisRef="Col.1.10">Col 1:10</reference>; this clause is connected with "that ye may be filled" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>), and "that ye may walk" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.10">Col 1:10</reference>).
