The connection is not, "We do not cease to pray for you (<reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>) giving thanks."<div eID="gen36253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36254" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the Father--</hi>of Jesus Christ, and so our Father by adoption (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.26">Ga 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4-Gal.4.6">4:4-6</reference>).<div eID="gen36254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which hath made us meet--</hi>Greek, "who made us meet." Not "is making us meet" by progressive growth in holiness; but once for all made us meet. It is not primarily the Spirit's work that is meant here, as the text is often used; but the Father's work in putting us by adoption, once for all, in a new standing, namely, that of children. The believers meant here were in different stages of progressive sanctification; but in respect to the meetness specified here, they all alike had it from the Father, in Christ His Son, being "complete in Him" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.10">Col 2:10</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="John.17.17">Joh 17:17</reference>; Jude 1, "sanctified by God the Father"; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>. Still, secondarily, this once-for-all meetness contains in it the germ of sanctification, afterwards developed progressively in the life by the Father's Spirit in the believer. The Christian life of heavenliness is the first stage of heaven itself. There must, and will be, a personal meetness for heaven, where there is a judicial meetness.<div eID="gen36255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be partakers, &c.--</hi>Greek, "for the (or 'our') portion of the inheritance (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.32">Ac 20:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">26:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.11">Ep 1:11</reference>) of the saints in light." "Light" begins in the believer here, descending from "the Father of lights" by Jesus, "the true light," and is perfected in the kingdom of light, which includes knowledge, purity, love, and joy. It is contrasted here with the "darkness" of the unconverted state (<reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen36256" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf54696c62375ae63248079643caddc8d11ada17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17837"/><div sID="gen36257" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17837"/><hi type="bold">13. from--</hi>Greek, "out of the power," out of the sphere in which his power is exercised.<div eID="gen36257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>blindness, hatred, misery [Bengel].<div eID="gen36258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">translated--</hi>Those thus translated as to state, are also transformed as to character. Satan has an organized dominion with various orders of powers of evil (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">6:12</reference>). But the term "kingdom" is rarely applied to his usurped rule (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.26">Mt 12:26</reference>); it is generally restricted to the kingdom of God.<div eID="gen36259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his dear Son--</hi>rather as Greek, "the Son of His love": the Son on whom His love rests (<reference osisRef="John.17.26">Joh 17:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>): contrasted with the "darkness" where all is hatred and hateful. <div eID="gen36260" type="x-p"/>
entries.858757953d177773c7601684d37ffa324977f2d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17838"/><div sID="gen36261" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17838"/>14. (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen36261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redemption--</hi>rather as Greek, "our redemption."<div eID="gen36262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through his blood--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts; probably inserted from <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>.<div eID="gen36263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sins--</hi>Translate as Greek, "our sins." The more general term: for which <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>, Greek, has, "our transgressions," the more special term. <div eID="gen36264" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec8c2d80480269fac576898ed308bcc9237d4344: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17839"/><div sID="gen36265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17839"/>15. They who have experienced in themselves "redemption" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.14">Col 1:14</reference>), know Christ in the glorious character here described, as above the highest angels to whom the false teachers (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>) taught worship was to be paid. Paul describes Him: (1) in relation to God and creation (Col 1:15-17); (2) in relation to the Church (<reference osisRef="Col.1.18-Col.1.20">Col 1:18-20</reference>). As the former regards Him as the Creator (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>) and the Sustainer (<reference osisRef="Col.1.17">Col 1:17</reference>) of the natural world; so the latter, as the source and stay of the new moral creation.<div eID="gen36265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">image--</hi>exact likeness and perfect Representative. Adam was made "in the image of God" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Ge 1:27</reference>). But Christ, the second Adam, perfectly reflected visibly "the invisible God" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Ti 1:17</reference>), whose glories the first Adam only in part represented. "Image" (eicon) involves "likeness" (homoiosis); but "likeness" does not involve "image." "Image" always supposes a prototype, which it not merely resembles, but from which it is drawn: the exact counterpart, as the reflection of the sun in the water: the child the living image of the parent. "Likeness" implies mere resemblance, not the exact counterpart and derivation as "image" expresses; hence it is nowhere applied to the Son, while "image" is here, compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.7">1Co 11:7</reference> [Trench]. (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.9">14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). Even before His incarnation He was the image of the invisible God, as the Word (<reference osisRef="John.1.1-John.1.3">Joh 1:1-3</reference>) by whom God created the worlds, and by whom God appeared to the patriarchs. Thus His essential character as always "the image of God," (1) before the incarnation, (2) in the days of His flesh, and (3) now in His glorified state, is, I think, contemplated here by the verb "is."<div eID="gen36266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first-born of every creature--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>), "the first-begotten": "begotten of His Father before all worlds" [Nicene Creed]. Priority and superlative dignity is implied (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Psa 89:27</reference>). English Version might seem to favor Arianism, as if Christ were a creature. Translate, "Begotten (literally, 'born') before every creature," as the context shows, which gives the reason why He is so designated. "For," &c. (<reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>) [Trench]. This expression is understood by Origen (so far is the Greek from favoring Socinian or Arian views) as declaring the Godhead of Christ, and is used by Him as a phrase to mark that Godhead, in contrast with His manhood [Book 2, sec. Against Celsus]. The Greek does not strictly admit Alford's translation, "the first-born of all creation." <div eID="gen36267" type="x-p"/>
entries.c63f7e09d83e25ef05490db8844911bd92ee8419: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17840"/><div sID="gen36268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17840"/><hi type="bold">16. For--</hi>Greek, "Because." This gives the proof that He is not included in the things created, but is the "first-begotten" before "every creature" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>), begotten as "the Son of God's love" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>), antecedently to all other emanations: "for" all these other emanations came from Him, and whatever was created, was created by Him.<div eID="gen36268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by him--</hi>rather as Greek, "in Him": as the conditional element, pre-existent and all-including: the creation of all things BY Him is expressed afterwards, and is a different fact from the present one, though implied in it [Alford]. God revealed Himself in the Son, the Word of the Father, before all created existence (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>). That Divine Word carries IN Himself the archetypes of all existences, so that "IN Him all things that are in heaven and earth have been created." The "in Him" indicates that the Word is the ideal ground of all existence; the "by Him," below, that He is the instrument of actually realizing the divine idea [Neander]. His essential nature as the Word of the Father is not a mere appendage of His incarnation, but is the ground of it. The original relation of the Eternal Word to men "made in His image" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.27">Ge 1:27</reference>), is the source of the new relation to them by redemption, formed in His incarnation, whereby He restores them to His lost image. "In Him" implies something prior to "by" and "for Him" presently after: the three prepositions mark in succession the beginning, the progress, and the end [Bengel].<div eID="gen36269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things--</hi>Greek, "the universe of things." That the new creation is not meant in this verse (as Socinians interpret), is plain; for angels, who are included in the catalogue, were not new created by Christ; and he does not speak of the new creation till <reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>. The creation "of the things that are in the heavens" (so Greek) includes the creation of the heavens themselves: the former are rather named, since the inhabitants are more noble than their dwellings. Heaven and earth and all that is m them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.6">Ne 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.10.6">Re 10:6</reference>).<div eID="gen36270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">invisible--</hi>the world of spirits.<div eID="gen36271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thrones, or dominions--</hi>lordships: the thrones are the greater of the two.<div eID="gen36272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principalities, or powers--</hi>rather, "rules, or authorities": the former are stronger than the latter (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>). The latter pair refer to offices in respect to God's creatures: "thrones and dominions" express exalted relation to God, they being the chariots on which He rides displaying His glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>). The existence of various orders of angels is established by this passage.<div eID="gen36273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things--</hi>Greek, "the whole universe of things."<div eID="gen36274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were--</hi>rather, to distinguish the Greek aorist, which precedes from the perfect tense here, "have been created." In the former case the creation was viewed as a past act at a point of time, or as done once for all; here it is viewed, not merely as one historic act of creation in the past, but as the permanent result now and eternally continuing.<div eID="gen36275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by him--</hi>as the instrumental Agent (<reference osisRef="John.1.3">Joh 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen36276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for him--</hi>as the grand End of creation; containing in Himself the reason why creation is at all, and why it is as it is [Alford]. He is the final cause as well as the efficient cause. Lachmann's punctuation of <reference osisRef="Col.1.15-Col.1.18">Col 1:15-18</reference> is best, whereby "the first-born of every creature" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>) answers to "the first-born from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.18">Col 1:18</reference>), the whole forming one sentence with the words ("All things were created by Him and for Him, and He is before all things, and by Him all things consist, and He is the Head of the body, the Church") intervening as a parenthesis. Thus Paul puts first, the origination by Him of the natural creation; secondly, of the new creation. The parenthesis falls into four clauses, two and two: the former two support the first assertion, "the first-born of every creature"; the latter two prepare us for "the first-born from the dead"'; the former two correspond to the latter two in their form--"All things by Him ... and He is," and "By Him all things ... and He is." <div eID="gen36277" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6c4d5dbb9877d8f77f79323b14464e4813c0c5b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17841"/><div sID="gen36278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17841"/>17. (<reference osisRef="John.8.58">Joh 8:58</reference>.) Translate as Greek, "And He Himself (the great He) is (implying divine essential being) before all things," in time, as well as in dignity. Since He is before all things, He is before even time, that is, from eternity. Compare "the first-born of every creature" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by him--</hi>Greek, "IN Him" (as the conditional element of existence, <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>) [Alford].<div eID="gen36279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consist--</hi>"subsist." Not only are called into being from nothing, but are maintained in their present state. The Son of God is the Conserver, as well as the Creator of all things [Pearson]. Bengel less probably explains, "All things in Him come together into one system: the universe found its completion in Him" (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Is 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.13">Re 22:13</reference>). Compare as to God, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.36">Ro 11:36</reference>: similar language; therefore Christ must be God. <div eID="gen36280" type="x-p"/>
entries.2fbac0f3625e32155c0d0f94c5c92b485ecc7463: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17842"/><div sID="gen36281" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17842"/>18. Revelation of Christ to the Church and the new creation, as the Originator of both.<div eID="gen36281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>emphatical. Not angels in opposition to the false teachers' doctrine concerning angel-worship, and the power of Oeons or (imaginary) spirit emanations from God (<reference osisRef="Col.2.10">Col 2:10</reference>, 18).<div eID="gen36282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head of the body, the church--</hi>The Church is His body by virtue of His entering into communion corporeally with human nature [Neander], (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>). The same One who is the Head of all things and beings by creation, is also, by virtue of being "the first-born from the dead," and so "the first-fruits" of the new creation among men, the Head of the Church.<div eID="gen36283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who is--</hi>that is, in that He is the Beginning [Alford]. Rather, this is the beginning of a new paragraph. As the former paragraph, which related to His originating the physical creation, began with "Who is" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>); so this, which treats of His originating the new creation, begins with "who is"; a parenthesis preceding, which closes the former paragraph, that parenthesis (see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col 1:16</reference>), including from "all things were created by Him," to "Head of the body, the Church." The head of kings and high priests was anointed, as the seat of the faculties, the fountain of dignity, and original of all the members (according to Hebrew etymology). So Jesus by His unction was designated as the Head of the body, the Church.<div eID="gen36284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the beginning--</hi>namely, of the new creation, as of the old (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Pr 8:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.1.8">Re 1:8</reference>): the beginning of the Church of the first-born (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">He 12:23</reference>), as being Himself the "first-born from the dead" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.23">Ac 26:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">1Co 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.23">23</reference>). Christ's primogeniture is threefold: (1) From eternity the "first-begotten" of the Father (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>); (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>) As the first-born of His mother (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.25">Mt 1:25</reference>); (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference>) As the Head of the Church, mystically begotten of the Father, as it were to a new life, on the day of His resurrection, which is His "regeneration," even as His people's coming resurrection will be their "regeneration" (that is, the resurrection which was begun in the soul, extended to the body and to the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Ro 8:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">22</reference>) (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.33">Ac 13:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>). Sonship and resurrection are similarly connected (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Lu 20:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Ro 1:4</reference>; 8:23; <reference osisRef="1John.3.2">1Jo 3:2</reference>). Christ by rising from the dead is the efficient cause (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.22">1Co 15:22</reference>), as having obtained the power, and the exemplary cause, as being the pattern (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.13">Mi 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>), of our resurrection: the resurrection of "the Head" involves consequentially that of the members.<div eID="gen36285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that in all things--</hi>He resumes the "all things" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen36286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he might have the pre-eminence--</hi>Greek, "He Himself may (thus) become the One holding the first place," or, "take the precedency." Both ideas are included, priority in time and priority in dignity: now in the regenerated world, as before in the world of creation (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>). "Begotten before every creature, or "first-born of every creature" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Psa 89:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.13">Joh 3:13</reference>). <div eID="gen36287" type="x-p"/>
entries.da4967ef368295f46417cca6096805bba185e0f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17843"/><div sID="gen36288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17843"/>19. Greek, "(God) was well pleased," &c.<div eID="gen36288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in him--</hi>that is, in the Son (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all fulness--</hi>rather as Greek, "all the fulness," namely, of God, whatever divine excellence is in God the Father (<reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.19">Ep 3:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>; 3:34). The Gnostics used the term "fulness," for the assemblage of emanations, or angelic powers, coming from God. The Spirit presciently by Paul warns the Church, that the true "fulness" dwells in Christ alone. This assigns the reason why Christ takes precedence of every creature (<reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>). For two reasons Christ is Lord of the Church: (1) Because the fulness of the divine attributes (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>) dwells in Him, and so He has the power to govern the universe; (2) Because (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>) what He has done for the Church gives Him the right to preside over it.<div eID="gen36290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">should ... dwell--</hi>as in a temple (<reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>). This indwelling of the Godhead in Christ is the foundation of the reconciliation by Him [Bengel]. Hence the "and" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>) connects as cause and effect the two things, the Godhead in Christ, and the reconciliation by Christ. <div eID="gen36291" type="x-p"/>
entries.7536eedf14491429a8dd7a2d6b1d33b5fa3fbee6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17844"/><div sID="gen36292" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17844"/>20. The Greek order is, "And through Him (Christ) to reconcile again completely (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.2.16">Ep 2:16</reference>) all things (Greek, 'the whole universe of things') unto Himself (unto God the Father, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>), having made peace (God the Father having made peace) through the blood of His (Christ's) cross," that is, shed by Christ on the cross: the price and pledge of our reconciliation with God. The Scripture phrase, "God reconciles man to Himself," implies that He takes away by the blood of Jesus the barrier which God's justice interposes against man's being in union with God (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.18">2Co 5:18</reference>). So the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.4">1Sa 29:4</reference>, "Wherewith should he reconcile himself unto his master," that is, reconcile his master unto him by appeasing his wrath. So <reference osisRef="Matt.5.23">Mt 5:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.24">24</reference>.<div eID="gen36292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by him--</hi>"through Him" (the instrumental agent in the new creation, as in the original creation): emphatically repeated, to bring the person of Christ, as the Head of both creations alike, into prominence.<div eID="gen36293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things in earth ... in heaven--</hi>Good angels, in one sense, do not need reconciliation to God; fallen angels are excluded from it (Jude 6). But probably redemption has effects on the world of spirits unknown to us. Of course, His reconciling us, and His reconciling them, must be by a different process, as He took not on Him the nature of angels, so as to offer a propitiation for them. But the effect of redemption on them, as He is their Head as well as ours, is that they are thereby brought nearer God, and so gain an increase of blessedness [Alford], and larger views of the love and wisdom of God (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>). All creation subsists in Christ, all creation is therefore affected by His propitiation: sinful creation is strictly "reconciled" from its enmity; sinless creation, comparatively distant from His unapproachable purity (<reference osisRef="Job.4.18">Job 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.15">15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">25:5</reference>), is lifted into nearer participation of Him, and in this wider sense is reconciled. Doubtless, too, man's fall, following on Satan's fall, is a segment of a larger circle of evil, so that the remedy of the former affects the standing of angels, from among whom Satan and his host fell. Angels thereby having seen the magnitude of sin, and the infinite cost of redemption, and the exclusion of the fallen angels from it, and the inability of any creature to stand morally in his own strength, are now put beyond the reach of falling. Thus Bacon's definition of Christ's Headship holds good: "The Head of redemption to man; the Head of preservation to angels." Some conjecture that Satan, when unfallen, ruled this earth and the pre-Adamic animal kingdom: hence his malice against man who succeeded to the lordship of this earth and its animals, and hence, too, his assumption of the form of a serpent, the subtlest of the animal tribes. <reference osisRef="Luke.19.38">Lu 19:38</reference> states expressly "peace in heaven" as the result of finished redemption, as "peace on earth" was the result of its beginning at Jesus' birth (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Lu 2:14</reference>). Bengel explains the reconciliation to be that of not only God, but also angels, estranged from men because of man's enmity against God. <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference> accords with this: This is true, but only part of the truth: so Alford's view also is but part of the truth. An actual reconciliation or restoration of peace in heaven, as well as on earth, is expressed by Paul. As long as that blood of reconciliation was not actually shed, which is opposed (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">9</reference>) to the accusations of Satan, but was only in promise, Satan could plead his right against men before God day and night (<reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Re 12:10</reference>); hence he was in heaven till the ban on man was broken (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.10.18">Lu 10:18</reference>). So here; the world of earth and heaven owe to Christ alone the restoration of harmony after the conflict and the subjugation of all things under one Head (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.23">He 11:23</reference>). Sin introduced discord not only on earth, but also in heaven, by the fall of demons; it brought into the abodes of holy angels, though not positive, yet privative loss, a retardation of their highest and most perfect development, harmonious gradation, and perfect consummation. Angels were no more able than men by themselves to overcome the peace disturbers, and cast out the devils; it is only "by," or "through Him," and "the blood of His cross," that peace was restored even in heaven; it is only after Christ has obtained the victory fully and legally, that Michael (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.7-Rev.12.10">Re 12:7-10</reference>) and his angels can cast out of heaven Satan and his demons (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>). Thus the point of Paul's argument against angel-worship is, that angels themselves, like men, wholly depend on Christ, the sole and true object of worship [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen36294" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0d1f19fd48cd87d93405802d0e931eee55c6117: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17845"/><div sID="gen36295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17845"/>21. The Colossians are included in this general reconciliation (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Ep 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen36295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sometime--</hi>"once."<div eID="gen36296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alienated--</hi>from God and salvation: objectively banished from God, through the barrier which God's justice interposed against your sin: subjectively estranged through the alienation of your own wills from God. The former is the prominent thought (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.10">Ro 5:10</reference>), as the second follows, "enemies in your mind." "Actual alienation makes habitual 'enemies'" [Bengel].<div eID="gen36297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in your mind--</hi>Greek, "in your understanding" or "thought" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.3">Ep 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by wicked works--</hi>rather as Greek, "in your wicked works" (wicked works were the element in which your enmity subsisted).<div eID="gen36299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet now--</hi>Notwithstanding the former alienation, now that Christ has come, God hath completely reconciled, or restored to His friendship again (so the Greek, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). <div eID="gen36300" type="x-p"/>
entries.15cfb0e7a3bfd4048a7a99b84cd983af75cedb38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17846"/><div sID="gen36301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17846"/><hi type="bold">22. In the body of his flesh--</hi>the element in which His reconciling sufferings had place. Compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>, "afflictions of Christ in my flesh" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>). Angels who have not a "body of flesh" are not in any way our reconciling mediators, as your false teachers assert, but He, the Lord of angels, who has taken our flesh, that in it He might atone for our fallen manhood.<div eID="gen36301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through death--</hi>rather as Greek, "through His death" (which could only take place in a body like ours, of flesh, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>). This implies He took on Him our true and entire manhood. Flesh is the sphere in which His human sufferings could have place (compare <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Ep 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to present you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Ep 5:27</reference>). The end of His reconciling atonement by death.<div eID="gen36303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holy--</hi>positively; and in relation to God.<div eID="gen36304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unblamable ... unreprovable--</hi>negatively. "Without blemish" (as the former Greek word is translated as to Jesus, our Head, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1Pe 1:19</reference>) in one's self. Irreproachable (the Greek for the second word, one who gives no occasion for his being brought to a law court) is in relation to the world without. Sanctification, as the fruit, is here treated of; justification, by Christ's reconciliation, as the tree, having preceded (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; 5:26, 27; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>). At the same time, our sanctification is regarded here as perfect in Christ, into whom we are grafted at regeneration or conversion, and who is "made of God unto us (perfect) sanctification" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference>; Jude 1): not merely progressive sanctification, which is the gradual development of the sanctification which Christ is made to the believer from the first.<div eID="gen36305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his sight--</hi>in God's sight, at Christ's appearing. <div eID="gen36306" type="x-p"/>
entries.70c32c01da86ee7510611e626c40d089be2fe844: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17847"/><div sID="gen36307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17847"/><hi type="bold">23. If--</hi>"Assuming that," &c.: not otherwise shall ye be so presented at His appearing (<reference osisRef="Col.1.22">Col 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen36307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grounded--</hi>Greek, "founded," "fixed on the foundation" (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Ep 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.48">Lu 6:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.49">49</reference>).<div eID="gen36308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">settled--</hi>"steadfast." "Grounded" respects the foundation on which believers rest; "settled," their own steadfastness (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.10">1Pe 5:10</reference>). <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.58">1Co 15:58</reference> has the same Greek.<div eID="gen36309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not moved away--</hi>by the false teachers.<div eID="gen36310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the hope of the gospel--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen36311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which ye have heard ... which was preached to every creature ... whereof I ... am ... a minister--</hi>Three arguments against their being "moved away from the Gospel": (1) Their having heard it; (2) The universality of the preaching of it; (3) Paul's ministry in it. For "to (Greek, 'in') every creature," the oldest manuscripts read, "in all creation." Compare "in all the world," <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference>; "all things ... in earth," <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference> (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.15">Mr 16:15</reference>): thus he implies that the Gospel from which he urges them not to be moved, has this mark of truth, namely, the universality of its announcement, which accords with the command and prophecy of Christ Himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Mt 24:14</reference>). By "was preached," he means not merely "is being preached," but has been actually, as an accomplished fact, preached. Pliny, not many years subsequently, in his famous letter to the Emperor Trajan [Epistles, Book X., Epistle 97], writes, "Many of every age, rank, and sex, are being brought to trial. For the contagion of that superstition [Christianity] has spread over not only cities, but villages and the country."<div eID="gen36312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereof I Paul am--</hi>rather as Greek, "was made a minister." Respect for me, the minister of this world-wide Gospel, should lead you not to be moved from it. Moreover (he implies), the Gospel which ye heard from Epaphras, your "minister" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.7">Col 1:7</reference>), is the same of which "I was made a minister" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.7">Ep 3:7</reference>): if you be moved from it, ye will desert the teaching of the recognized ministers of the Gospel for unauthorized false teachers. <div eID="gen36313" type="x-p"/>
entries.b27203dcf32dd96eccef30b93b525624abbad0bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17848"/><div sID="gen36314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17848"/><hi type="bold">24. Who--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "who"; then translate, "Now I rejoice." Some very old manuscripts, and the best of the Latin versions, and Vulgate, read as English Version. To enhance the glory of Christ as paramount to all, he mentions his own sufferings for the Church of Christ. "Now" stands in contrast to "I was made," in the past time (<reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>).<div eID="gen36314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>"on your behalf," that ye may be confirmed in resting solely on Christ (to the exclusion of angel-worship) by the glorification of Christ in my sufferings (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.1">Ep 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill up that which is behind--</hi>literally, "the deficiencies"--all that are lacking of the afflictions of Christ (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2Co 1:5</reference>). Christ is "afflicted in all His people's afflictions" (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>). "The Church is His body in which He is, dwells, lives, and therefore also suffers" [Vitringa]. Christ was destined to endure certain afflictions in this figurative body, as well as in His literal; these were "that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ," which Paul "filled up." His own meritorious sufferings in expiation for sin were once for all completely filled up on the Cross. But His Church (His second Self) has her whole measure of afflictions fixed. The more Paul, a member, endured, the less remain for the rest of the Church to endure; the communion of saints thus giving them an interest in his sufferings. It is in reference to the Church's afflictions, which are "Christ's afflictions, that Paul here saith, "I fill up the deficiencies," or "what remain behind of the afflictions of Christ." She is afflicted to promote her growth in holiness, and her completeness in Christ. Not one suffering is lost (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>). All her members have thus a mutual interest in one another's sufferings (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.26">1Co 12:26</reference>). But Rome's inference hence, is utterly false that the Church has a stock treasury of the merits and satisfactions of Christ and His apostles, out of which she may dispense indulgences; the context has no reference to sufferings in expiation of sin and productive of merit. Believers should regard their sufferings less in relation to themselves as individuals, and more as parts of a grand whole, carrying out God's perfect plan. <div eID="gen36316" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea4805a8a8254e70549d51fbc2f166b4903d5850: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17849"/><div sID="gen36317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17849"/><hi type="bold">25. am--</hi>Greek, "I was made a minister": resuming <reference osisRef="Col.1.23">Col 1:23</reference>, "whereof I Paul was made a minister."<div eID="gen36317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dispensation--</hi>the stewardship committed to me to dispense in the house of God, the Church, to the whole family of believers, the goods of my Master (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.42">Lu 12:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">1Co 4:1</reference>, 2; 9:17; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.2">Ep 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which is given--</hi>Greek, "which was given."<div eID="gen36319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>with a view to you, Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.15.16">Ro 15:16</reference>).<div eID="gen36320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to fulfil--</hi>to bring it fully to all: the end of his stewardship: "fully preached" (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Ro 15:19</reference>). "The fulness of Christ (<reference osisRef="Col.1.19">Col 1:19</reference>), and of the times (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>) required him so to do" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen36321" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcfbae867bb6a3dbc43adcf35e359adc34466d26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17850"/><div sID="gen36322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17850"/><hi type="bold">26. the mystery--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.9">Ep 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.5-Eph.3.9">Ep 3:5-9</reference>). The mystery, once hidden, now revealed, is redemption for the whole Gentile world, as well as for the Jews, "Christ in you (Gentiles) the hope of glory" (<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>).<div eID="gen36322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ages--</hi>"from," according to Alford, refers to time, not "hidden from": from the time of the ages; still what is meant is that the mystery was hidden from the beings living in those "ages." The "ages" are the vast successive periods marked by successive orders of beings and stages of creation. Greek, "Æons," a word used by the Gnostics for angelic beings emanating from God. The Spirit by Paul presciently, in opposition to Gnostic error already beginning (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>), teaches, that the mystery of redemption was hidden in God's purposes in Christ, alike from the angelic beings (compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Ep 3:10</reference>) of the pre-Adamic "ages," and from the subsequent human "generations." Translate as Greek, "the ages ... the generations."<div eID="gen36323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made manifest to his saints--</hi>to His apostles and prophets primarily (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>), and through them to all His saints. <div eID="gen36324" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1040788004efeab3c0222f69d466ab3ef9532f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17851"/><div sID="gen36325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17851"/><hi type="bold">27. would--</hi>rather as Greek, "willed," or "was pleased to make known." He resolves all into God's good pleasure and will, that man should not glory save in God's grace.<div eID="gen36325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what--</hi>How full and inexhaustible!<div eID="gen36326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the riches of the glory of this mystery--</hi>He accumulates phrase on phrase to enhance the greatness of the blessing in Christ bestowed by God on the Gentiles. Compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>, "all the treasures" of wisdom; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Ep 3:8</reference>, "the unsearchable riches of Christ"; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Ep 1:7</reference>, "riches of His grace." "The glory of this mystery" must be the glory which this once hidden, and now revealed, truth makes you Gentiles partakers of, partly now, but mainly when Christ shall come (<reference osisRef="Col.3.4">Col 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.2">Ro 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>). This sense is proved by the following: "Christ in you the hope of the (so Greek) glory." The lower was the degradation of you Gentiles, the higher is the richness of the glory to which the mystery revealed now raises you. You were "without Christ, and having no hope" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.12">Ep 2:12</reference>). Now you have "Christ in you the hope of the glory" just mentioned. Alford translates, "Christ among you," to answer to "this mystery among the Gentiles." But the whole clause, "Christ IN you (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.17">Ep 3:17</reference>) the hope of glory," answers to "this mystery," and not to the whole sentence, "this mystery among the Gentiles." What is made known "among you Gentiles" is, "Christ in you (now by faith as your hidden life, <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>) the hope of glory" (your manifested life). The contrast (antithesis) between "Christ in you" now as your hidden life, and "the hope of glory" hereafter to be manifested, requires this translation. <div eID="gen36327" type="x-p"/>
entries.84a10b29b0f57d65a09323ca93c49f5c0b431421: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17852"/><div sID="gen36328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17852"/><hi type="bold">28. preach--</hi>rather as Greek, "announce" or "proclaim."<div eID="gen36328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">warning ... teaching--</hi>"Warning" is connected with repentance, refers to one's conduct, and is addressed primarily to the heart. "Teaching" is connected with faith, refers to doctrines, and is addressed primarily to the intellect. These are the two heads of evangelical teaching.<div eID="gen36329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every ... every man--</hi>without distinction of Jew or Gentile, great or small (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.12">Ro 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen36330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all wisdom--</hi>with all the wisdom in our method of teaching that we possess: so Alford. But <reference osisRef="Col.1.9">Col 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>, favor Estius' view, which refers it to the wisdom communicated to those being taught: keeping back nothing, but instructing all in the perfect knowledge of the mysteries of faith which is the true wisdom (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.8">12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen36331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">present--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Col.1.22">Col 1:22</reference>); at Christ's coming.<div eID="gen36332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every man--</hi>Paul is zealous lest the false teachers should seduce one single soul of Christ's people at Colosse. So each individual among them should be zealous for himself and his neighbor. Even one soul is of incalculable value.<div eID="gen36333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect in Christ--</hi>who is the element in living union with whom alone each believer can find perfection: perfectly instructed (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.13">Ep 4:13</reference>) in doctrine, and full grown or matured in faith and practice. "Jesus" is omitted in all the oldest manuscripts. <div eID="gen36334" type="x-p"/>
entries.38b0bff9f622f59af0c47638c439018fc4981939: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17853"/><div sID="gen36335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17853"/><hi type="bold">29. Whereunto--</hi>namely, "to present every man perfect in Christ."<div eID="gen36335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I also labour--</hi>rather, "I labor also." I not only "proclaim" (English Version, "preach") Christ, but I labor also.<div eID="gen36336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">striving--</hi>in "conflict" (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>) of spirit (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>). The same Greek word is used of Epaphras (<reference osisRef="Col.4.12">Col 4:12</reference>), "laboring fervently for you in prayers": literally, "agonizing," "striving as in the agony of a contest." So Jesus in Gethsemane when praying (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.44">Lu 22:44</reference>): so "strive" (the same Greek word, "agonize"), <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Lu 13:24</reference>. So Jacob "wrestled" in prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24-Gen.32.29">Ge 32:24-29</reference>). Compare "contention," Greek, "agony," or "striving earnestness," <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.2">1Th 2:2</reference>.<div eID="gen36337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to his working--</hi>Paul avows that he has power to "strive" in spirit for his converts, so far only as Christ works in him and by him (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Ep 3:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.13">Php 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mightily--</hi>literally, "in power." <chapter eID="Col.1"/>

entries.e9c3e477b1126c775633db0d19492f2154167898: <div eID="gen50756" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Colossians</title> <div sID="gen50757" type="x-p"/> Colosse, or rather Colassa, (see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col 1:1</reference> (note)), was a city of Phrygia Pacatiana, now a part of Natolia, in Asia Minor, seated on an eminence on the south side of the river Maeander, now Meinder, near to the place where the river Lycas enters the earth, and begins to run under ground, which course it continues for about three-quarters of a mile, before it emerges and falls into the Maeander. Of this ancient city not much is known: it was situated between Laodicea and Hierapolis, and at an equal distance from either; and to this place Xerxes came in his expedition against Greece. <div eID="gen50757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50758" type="x-p"/> The government of this city is said to have been democratic, and its first magistrate bore the title of archon and praetor. The Macedonians transferred Colosse to the Persians; and it afterwards passed under the government of the Seleucidae. After the defeat of Antiochus III., at the battle of Magnesia, it became subject to Eumenes, king of Pergamus: and when Attalus, the last of his successors, bequeathed his dominions to the Romans, this city, with the whole of Phrygia, formed a part of the proconsular province of Asia; which division subsisted till the time of Constantine the Great. After the time of this emperor, Phrygia was divided into Phrygia Pacatiana, and Phrygia Salutaris: and Colosse was the sixth city of the first division. <div eID="gen50758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50759" type="x-p"/> The ancient city of Colosse has been extinct for nearly eighteen hundred years; for about the tenth year of the Emperor Nero, about a year after the writing of this epistle, not only Colosse, but Laodicea and Hierapolis, were destroyed by an earthquake, according to Eusebius; and the city which was raised in the place of the former was called Chonos or Konos, which name it now bears. See New Encyclopedia. On modern maps Konos is situated about twenty miles NE. of Degnizlu, in lat. about 38 north, and in long. 29 40' east of London. <div eID="gen50759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50760" type="x-p"/> The epistle to this city appears to have been written about the same time with that to the Philippians, viz. towards the end of the year 62, and in the ninth of the Emperor Nero. <div eID="gen50760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50761" type="x-p"/> That the two epistles were written about the same time is rendered probable by the following circumstance: In the Epistle to the Philippians, <reference osisRef="Phi.2.19">Phi 2:19</reference>, St. Paul purposes to send Timothy to Philippi, who was then with him at Rome, that he might know their state. As Timothy joins with the apostle in the salutation at the beginning of this epistle, it is evident that he was still at Rome, and had not yet been sent to Philippi; and as St. Paul wrote the former epistle nearly at the close of his first imprisonment at Rome, the two epistles must have been written within a short space of each other. See the preface to the Epistle to the Philippians. <div eID="gen50761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50762" type="x-p"/> When, or by whom, Christianity was first preached at Colosse, and a Church founded there, we cannot tell; but it is most likely that it was by St. Paul himself, and during the three years in which he dwelt at Ephesus; for he had then employed himself with such zeal and diligence that we are told, <reference osisRef="Act.19.10">Act 19:10</reference> : "That all they that dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks." And that Paul preached in Phrygia, the district in which this city was situated, we learn from <reference osisRef="Act.16.6">Act 16:6</reference> : "Now when they had gone through Phrygia and the region of Galatia;" and at another time we find that "he went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples;" <reference osisRef="Act.18.23">Act 18:23</reference>. It has, however, been argued, from <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>, of this epistle, that Paul had never been at Colosse; for he there says: I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh. But the consequence drawn from these words does not absolutely follow. Dr. Lardner alleges a variety of considerations which induced him to believe that the Churches of Colosse and Laodicea were founded by St. Paul, viz. <div eID="gen50762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50763" type="x-p"/> 1. That the apostle was twice in Phrygia, in which were Colosse, Laodicea, and Hierapolis. See the places above quoted from the Acts of the Apostles. <div eID="gen50763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50764" type="x-p"/> 2. That he does in effect, or even expressly, say that he had dispensed the Gospel to the Colossians, <reference osisRef="Col.1.21-Col.1.25">Col 1:21-25</reference>. See particularly the 23rd, 24th, and 25th verses. <div eID="gen50764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50765" type="x-p"/> 3. From several passages in the epistle it appears that the apostle does not speak as to strangers, but to acquaintances, disciples, and converts. Some think that Epaphras, who is called their apostle, <reference osisRef="Col.1.7">Col 1:7</reference>, was the first who planted Christianity among the Colossians. <div eID="gen50765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50766" type="x-p"/> But the arguments drawn from <reference osisRef="Act.16.6">Act 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.18.23">Act 18:23</reference>, referred to above, are quite invalidated, if we allow the opinion of some learned men, among whom are Suidas, Calepine, Munster, and others, that the Colossus, a gigantic statue at Rhodes, gave its own name to the people among whom it stood; for the ancient poets call the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes, Colossians; and hence they thought that the Colossians, to whom St. Paul directs this epistle, were the inhabitants of Rhodes. This opinion, however, is not generally adopted. From a great similarity in the doctrine and phraseology of this epistle to that written to the Ephesians, this to the Colossians has been considered an epitome of the former, as the Epistle to the Galatians has been considered an abstract of that to the Romans. See the concluding observations on the Epistle to the Galatians (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Gal 5:17</reference> (note)); and the notes on <reference osisRef="Col.1.4">Col 1:4</reference> (note), and elsewhere. <div eID="gen50766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50767" type="x-p"/> Whether the Colossians to whom the apostle addresses this epistle were Jews or Gentiles, cannot be absolutely determined. It is most probable that they were a mixture of both; but that the principal part were converted Jews is most likely. This, indeed, appears to have been the case in most of the Asiatic and Grecian Churches; for there were Jews, at this time, sojourning in almost every part of the Roman empire, which then comprehended the greatest portion of the known world. <div eID="gen50767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50768" type="x-p"/> The language of this epistle is bold and energetic, the sentiments are grand, and the conceptions vigorous and majestic. The phraseology is in many places Jewish; and the reason is obvious: the apostle had to explain subjects which never had a name in any other language. The mythology of the Gentiles could not furnish terms to explain the theology of the Jews; much less, the more refined and spiritual system of Christianity. <div eID="gen50768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50769" type="x-p"/> The salutation of Paul and Timothy to the Church at Colosse, <reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.2">Col 1:2</reference>. They give thanks to God for the good estate of that Church, and the wonderful progress of the Gospel in every place, <reference osisRef="Col.1.3-Col.1.6">Col 1:3-6</reference>; having received particulars of their state from Epaphroditus, which not only excited their gratitude, but led them to pray to God that they might walk worthy of the Gospel; and they give thanks to Him who had made them meet for an inheritance among the saints in light, <reference osisRef="Col.1.7-Col.1.12">Col 1:7-12</reference>. This state is described as a deliverance from the power of darkness, and being brought into the kingdom of God's dear Son, <reference osisRef="Col.1.13">Col 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.14">Col 1:14</reference>. The glorious character of Jesus Christ, and what He has done for mankind, <reference osisRef="Col.1.15-Col.1.20">Col 1:15-20</reference>. The salvation which the Colossians had received, and of which the apostle had been the minister and dispenser, <reference osisRef="Col.1.21-Col.1.26">Col 1:21-26</reference>. The sum and substance of the apostle's preaching, and the manner in which he executed his ministry, <reference osisRef="Col.1.27-Col.1.29">Col 1:27-29</reference>. <div eID="gen50769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50770" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50771" type="x-p"/> Paul, an apostle - by the will of God - As the word αποστολος, apostle, signifies one sent, an envoy or messenger, any person or persons may be the senders: but the word is particularly restrained to the messengers of the everlasting Gospel, sent immediately from God himself; and this is what St. Paul particularly remarks here when he calls himself an apostle by the will of God; signifying that he had derived his commission from an express volition or purpose of the Almighty. <div eID="gen50771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50772" type="x-p"/> And Timotheus - Though Timothy is here joined in the salutation, yet he has never been understood as having any part in composing this epistle. He has been considered as the amanuensis or scribe of the apostle.
entries.b300a133d58425f28a44186ab87391d54a5f2265: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50773" type="x-p"/> To the saints - Those who professed Christianity. See the note on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Eph 1:1</reference>. <div eID="gen50773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50774" type="x-p"/> Which are at Colosse - Instead of εν Κολοσσαις, at Colosse, or among the Colossians, ABC, and many other excellent MSS., with both the Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic, Origen, Gregory Nyssen, Amphilochus, Theodoret, Damascenus, Theophylact, and others, read εν Κολασσαις in Colassa, or among the Colassians; and this is most probably the true reading. That this city perished by an earthquake, a short time after the date of this epistle, we have the testimony of Eusebius. That which at present is supposed to occupy the site of this ancient city is called Konos. For other particulars see the preface to this epistle. <div eID="gen50774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50775" type="x-p"/> Grace be unto you - See on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.7">Rom 1:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen50775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50776" type="x-p"/> And the Lord Jesus Christ - This clause is omitted by many MSS., several versions, and some of the fathers. Griesbach has left it out of the text, not, in my opinion, on sufficient evidence.
entries.ff9e05602eb6fec970bda514862af6b3e62ba002: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen50776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50777" type="x-p"/> We give thanks to God - Who is the author of all good; and from whom the grace, which has produced your conversion, has sprung by his mission of Christ Jesus. See the note on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15">Eph 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.16">Eph 1:16</reference> (note).
entries.b646fcc06b2439f646ec34a438c99e082fca3a09: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen50777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50778" type="x-p"/> Since we heard of your faith - This is very similar to <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15">Eph 1:15</reference>. And it is certain that the apostle seems to have considered the Church at Ephesus, and that at Colassa to have been nearly in the same state, as the two epistles are very similar in their doctrine and phraseology.
entries.1218068b1cd1b02646b640a01c857a0f3ce3d9d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen50778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50779" type="x-p"/> Which is come unto you - The doctrine of the Gospel is represented as a traveler, whose object it is to visit the whole habitable earth; and, having commenced his journey in Judea, had proceeded through Syria and through different parts of Asia Minor, and had lately arrived at their city, every where proclaiming glad tidings of great joy to all people. <div eID="gen50779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50780" type="x-p"/> As it is in all the world - So rapid is this traveler in his course, that he had already gone nearly through the whole of the countries under the Roman dominion; and will travel on till he has proclaimed his message to every people, and kindred, and nation, and tongue. <div eID="gen50780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50781" type="x-p"/> In the beginning of the apostolic age, the word of the Lord had certainly free course, did run and was glorified. Since that time the population of the earth has increased greatly; and, to follow the metaphor, the traveler still continues in his great journey. It is, the glory of the present day that, by means of the British and Foreign Bible Society, Bibles are multiplied in all the languages of Europe; and by means of the Christian missionaries, Carey, Marshman, and Ward, whose zeal, constancy, and ability, have been rarely equalled, and perhaps never surpassed, the sacred writings have been, in the compass of a few years, translated into most of the written languages of India, in which they were not previously extant. In this labor they have been ably seconded by the Rev. Henry Martyn, one of the East India Company's chaplains, who was taken to his great reward just when he had completed a pure and accurate version of the New Testament into Persian. The Rev. R. Morrison, at Canton, has had the honor to present the whole of the New Testament, in Chinese, to the immense population of that greatest empire of the earth. May that dark people receive it, and walk in the light of the Lord! And, by means of the Wesleyan missionaries, the sacred writings have been printed and widely circulated in the Singhalese and Indo- Portuguese, through the whole of the island of Ceylon, and the pure word of the Gospel has been preached there, and also on the whole continent of India, to the conversion of multitudes. Let every reader pray that all these noble attempts may be crowned with unlimited success, till the earth is filled both with the knowledge and glory of the Lord. Talia secla currite! Amen. <div eID="gen50781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50782" type="x-p"/> And bringeth forth fruit - Wherever the pure Gospel of Christ is preached, it is the seed of the kingdom, and must be fruitful in all those who receive it by faith, in simplicity of heart. <div eID="gen50782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50783" type="x-p"/> After καρποφορουμενον, bringeth forth fruit, ABCD*EFG, many others, both the Syriac, Erpen's Arabic, the Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Slavonic, Vulgate, and Itala, together with many of the fathers, add και αυξανομενον, and increaseth. It had not only brought forth fruit, but was multiplying its own kind; every fruit containing seed, and every seed producing thirty, sixty, or a hundredfold. This reading is very important, and is undoubtedly genuine. <div eID="gen50783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50784" type="x-p"/> The grace of God in truth - Ye were fruitful, and went on increasing in the salvation of God, from the time that ye heard and acknowledged this doctrine to be of God, to spring from the grace or benevolence of God; and received it in truth, sincerely and uprightly, as his greatest gift to man.
entries.4f5e569bf15c66fb2e93782091af1c371e832a9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen50784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50785" type="x-p"/> As ye also learned of Epaphras - who is for you - Who this Epaphras was we cannot tell; only it is likely that he was a Colossian, and became, by the call and grace of Christ, a deacon of this Church, faithfully labouring with the apostle, to promote its best interests. Some think that he is the same with Epaphroditus, Epaphras being a contraction of that name, as Demas is of Demetrius; and it is remarkable that one of the Slavonic versions has Epaphroditus in this place. That he was a Colossian is evident from <reference osisRef="Col.4.12">Col 4:12</reference> : Epaphras, who is one of you, ὁ εξ ὑμων· some think that he was the first who preached the Gospel among this people, and hence called an apostle. He was raised up among themselves to be their minister in the absence of the apostle, and he showed himself to be worthy of this calling by a faithful discharge of his ministry, and by labouring fervently for them all, and pressing them forward, that they might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
entries.35ce275f3ecae3f93c31feaa1e773cf774409615: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen50785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50786" type="x-p"/> Your love in the Spirit - So we preached, and so ye believed. The heavenly flame in the heart of this minister communicated itself to those who heard him; it was like priest like people. They enjoyed a spiritual, energetic ministry, and they were a spiritual people; they had a loving spirit, and love through the Spirit of God which dwelt in them. And of this love of theirs in the Spirit, and particularly towards the apostle, Epaphras gave full proof, not only by describing to the apostle the affection they felt for him, but in presenting to him those supplies which their love to him caused them to furnish.
entries.4e7c7ebd3c5f477b6064ce1e0d291824a4f46652: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen50786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50787" type="x-p"/> For this cause - See on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.15-Eph.1.16">Eph 1:15-16</reference> (note), where the same sentiment occurs. <div eID="gen50787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50788" type="x-p"/> That ye might be filled - Nothing could satisfy the apostle, either for himself or his hearers, but the fullness of the blessing of the Gospel of peace. The Colossians had knowledge, but they must have more; it is their privilege to be filled with it. As the bright shining of the sun in the firmament of heaven fills the whole world with light and heat, so the light of the Sun of righteousness is to illuminate their whole souls, and fill them with Divine splendor, so that they might know the will of God, in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; in a word, that they might have such a knowledge of Divine things as the Spirit of truth can teach to the soul of man.
entries.c23129c26685171f8c0de2cef2e1dbef022ff406: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen50788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50789" type="x-p"/> That ye might walk worthy of the Lord - Suitably to your Christian profession, exemplifying its holy doctrines by a holy and useful life. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Eph 4:1</reference>; and on <reference osisRef="Phi.1.27">Phi 1:27</reference> (note). <div eID="gen50789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50790" type="x-p"/> Unto all pleasing - Doing every thing in the best manner, in the most proper time, and in a becoming spirit. Even a good work may be marred and rendered fruitless by being done improperly, out of season, or in a temper of mind that grieves the Holy Spirit. <div eID="gen50790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50791" type="x-p"/> Being fruitful in every good work - See on <reference osisRef="Col.1.6">Col 1:6</reference> (note). St. Paul exhorts the Christians at Colosse, <div eID="gen50791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50792" type="x-p"/> 1. To walk - to be active in their Christian calling. <div eID="gen50792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50793" type="x-p"/> 2. To walk worthily - suitably to the dignity of that calling, and to the purity of that God who had called them into this state of salvation. <div eID="gen50793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50794" type="x-p"/> 3. To do every thing unto all pleasing; that God might be pleased with the manner, the time, the motive, disposition, design, and object of every act. <div eID="gen50794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50795" type="x-p"/> 4. That they should be fruitful; mere harmlessness would not be sufficient; as God had sown good seed, he expected good fruit. <div eID="gen50795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50796" type="x-p"/> 5. That every work should be good; they must not be fruitful in some works and fruitless in others. <div eID="gen50796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50797" type="x-p"/> 6. That they should increase in religious knowledge as time rolled on, knowing, by genuine Christian experience, more of God, of his love, and of his peace, day by day.
entries.d346df36b56ad6f074882bf492b5842704050ae3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen50797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50798" type="x-p"/> Strengthened with all might - That they might be able to walk worthy of the Lord, bring forth fruit, etc. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eph.3.13">Eph 3:13</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen50798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50799" type="x-p"/> According to his glorious power - According to that sufficiency of strength which may be expected from him who has all power both in the heavens and in the earth. <div eID="gen50799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50800" type="x-p"/> Unto all patience - Relieving, hoping, and enduring all things. <div eID="gen50800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50801" type="x-p"/> With joyfulness - Feeling the continual testimony that ye please God, which will be a spring of perpetual comfort. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eph.4.2">Eph 4:2</reference>.
entries.a585f8bc353753025c88fb05fd9746d396773791: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen50801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50802" type="x-p"/> Giving thanks unto the Father - Knowing that ye have nothing but what ye have received from his mere mercy, and that in point of merit ye can never claim any thing from him. <div eID="gen50802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50803" type="x-p"/> Which hath made us meet - Ἱκανωσαντι· Who has qualified us to be partakers, etc. Instead of ἱκανωσαντι, some MSS. and versions have καλεσαντι, called; and B (the Codex Vaticanus) has both readings. Giving thanks unto the Father, who hath called and qualified us to be partakers. <div eID="gen50803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50804" type="x-p"/> Of the inheritance - Εις την μεριδα του κληρου. A plain allusion to the division of the promised land by lot among the different families of the twelve Israelitish tribes. The κληρος was the lot or inheritance belonging to the tribe; the μερις was the portion in that lot which belonged to each family of that tribe. This was a type of the kingdom of God, in which portions of eternal blessedness are dispensed to the genuine Israelites; to them who have the circumcision of the heart by the Spirit, whose praise is of God, and not of man. <div eID="gen50804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50805" type="x-p"/> Of the saints in light - Light, in the sacred writings, is used to express knowledge, felicity, purity, comfort, and joy of the most substantial kind; here it is put to point out the state of glory at the right hand of God. As in Egypt, while the judgments of God were upon the land, there was a darkness which might be felt yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings; so in this world, while the darkness and wretchedness occasioned by sin remain, the disciples of Christ are light in the Lord, walk as children of the light and of the day, have in them no occasion of stumbling, and are on their way to the ineffable light at the right hand of God. Some think there is an allusion here to the Eleusinian mysteries, celebrated in deep caves and darkness in honor of Ceres; but I have already, in the notes to the Epistle to the Ephesians, expressed my doubts that the apostle has ever condescended to use such a simile. The phraseology of the text is frequent through various parts of the sacred writings, where it is most obvious that no such allusion could possibly be intended.
entries.daee38f16c35363bd16dfa6eb3fe5b3b709084bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen50805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50806" type="x-p"/> Delivered us from the power of darkness - Darkness is here personified, and is represented as having εξουσια, power, authority, and sway; all Jews and Gentiles, which had not embraced the Gospel, being under this authority and power. And the apostle intimates here that nothing less than the power of God can redeem a man from this darkness, or prince of darkness, who, by means of sin and unbelief, keeps men in ignorance, vice, and misery. <div eID="gen50806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50807" type="x-p"/> Translated us into the kingdom, etc - He has thoroughly changed our state, brought us out of the dark region of vice and impiety, and placed us in the kingdom under the government of his dear Son, Υἱου της αγαπης αὑτου, the Son of his love; the person whom, in his infinite love, he has given to make an atonement for the sin of the world.
entries.b28f9eb605c27f87036b6024350711179017a992: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen50807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50808" type="x-p"/> In whom we have redemption - Who has paid down the redemption price, even his own blood, that our sins might be cancelled, and we made fit to be partakers of the inheritance among the saints in light. <div eID="gen50808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50809" type="x-p"/> The clause, δια του αἱματος αυτου, Through his blood, is omitted by ABCDEFG, and by most others of weight and importance; by the Syriac, Arabic of Erpen, Coptic, Ethiopic, Sahidic, some copies of the Vulgate and by the Itala; and by most of the Greek fathers. Griesbach has left it out of the text. It is likely that the reading here is not genuine; yet that we have redemption any other way than through the sacrifice of Christ, the Scriptures declare not. The same phrase is used <reference osisRef="Eph.1.7">Eph 1:7</reference>, where there is no various reading in any of the MSS., versions, or fathers. <div eID="gen50809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50810" type="x-p"/> The forgiveness of sins - Αφεσιν των ἁμαρτιων· The taking away of sins; all the power, guilt, and infection of sin. All sin of every kind, with all its influence and consequences.
entries.2a682a5b9a7e7cb13d8ba44ca5810baf9ebcab18: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen50810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50811" type="x-p"/> Who is the image of the invisible God - The counterpart of God Almighty, and if the image of the invisible God, consequently nothing that appeared in him could be that image; for if it could be visible in the Son, it could also be visible in the Father; but if the Father be invisible, consequently his image in the Son must be invisible also. This is that form of God of which he divested himself; the ineffable glory in which he not only did not appear, as to its splendor and accompaniments, but concealed also its essential nature; that inaccessible light which no man, no created being, can possibly see. This was that Divine nature, the fullness of the Godhead bodily, which dwelt in him. <div eID="gen50811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50812" type="x-p"/> The first-born of every creature - I suppose this phrase to mean the same as that, <reference osisRef="Phi.2.9">Phi 2:9</reference> : God hath given him a name which is above every name; he is as man at the head of all the creation of God; nor can he with any propriety be considered as a creature, having himself created all things, and existed before any thing was made. If it be said that God created him first, and that he, by a delegated power from God, created all things, this is most flatly contradicted by the apostle's reasoning in the 16th and 17th verses. As the Jews term Jehovah בכורו של עולם becoro shel olam, the first-born of all the world, or of all the creation, to signify his having created or produced all things; (see Wolfius in loc.) so Christ is here termed, and the words which follow in the 16th and 17th verses are the proof of this. The phraseology is Jewish; and as they apply it to the supreme Being merely to denote his eternal pre-existence, and to point him out as the cause of all things; it is most evident that St. Paul uses it in the same way, and illustrates his meaning in the following words, which would be absolutely absurd if we could suppose that by the former he intended to convey any idea of the inferiority of Jesus Christ.
entries.88216938c5115cc1508b78983c66331ff0d566c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen50812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50813" type="x-p"/> For by him were all things created, etc - These two verses contain parts of the same subject. I shall endeavor to distinguish the statements of the apostle, and reason from them in such a way as the premises shall appear to justify, without appealing to any other scripture in proof of the doctrine which I suppose these verses to vindicate. <div eID="gen50813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50814" type="x-p"/> Four things are here asserted: <div eID="gen50814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50815" type="x-p"/> 1. That Jesus Christ is the Creator of the universe; of all things visible and invisible; of all things that had a beginning, whether they exist in time or in eternity. <div eID="gen50815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50816" type="x-p"/> 2. That whatsoever was created was created For himself; that he was the sole end of his own work. <div eID="gen50816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50817" type="x-p"/> 3. That he was prior to all creation, to all beings, whether in the visible or invisible world. <div eID="gen50817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50818" type="x-p"/> 4. That he is the preserver and governor of all things; for by him all things consist. <div eID="gen50818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50819" type="x-p"/> Now, allowing St. Paul to have understood the terms which he used, he must have considered Jesus Christ as being truly and properly God. <div eID="gen50819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50820" type="x-p"/> I.
